wavelet.explanation: Creates a synthetic uniform image (vtkImageData) whose point array RTData combines a Gaussian peak of height maximum with sinusoidal terms along x, y and z. With the Schemaxis defaults it is a 21 x 21 x 21-point grid with unit spacing spanning -10 to 10 on each axis. Use it as a self-contained input to try slice, contour, clip, streamTracer or scene settings without a real case; its values have no physical meaning or units.

examples.purpose: Extract a plane through an analytic wavelet.

pitfalls: Each extent minimum must be smaller than its maximum, so the curated wavelet cannot produce a 2-D image; use pvWavelet for planar or subsampled images and to change frequencies, amplitudes or the Gaussian width.
RTData is a scalar; derive test vectors with calculator (e.g. iHat), as the native acceptance example examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json does before its analytic integral checks.

sphere.explanation: Creates a triangulated polygonal sphere (vtkPolyData with point normals) of given radius about centre, with its poles on the z axis. resolution sets the number of longitude divisions around z (Schemaxis default 24, ParaView's own default 8); latitude divisions are fixed at 24 by Schemaxis. Use it as a marker, a target mesh for resample, a seed surface for streamTracer or simple test geometry; its coordinates are in the units of the data it is combined with.
pitfalls: Latitude resolution (PhiResolution) is fixed at 24, so a very high resolution gives long thin facets; use pvSphere to set ThetaResolution and PhiResolution together or to make a partial sphere.
The facets lie inside the true sphere, so the surface area and enclosed volume are slightly smaller than the analytic values, noticeably so at low resolution.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, with the default options; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

line.explanation: Creates a straight polyline from start to end with resolution intervals (Schemaxis default 20, so 21 points), as a separate polydata source. Connect it to streamTracer.seed to place streamline seeds, or use it as probe geometry; it is not the velocity dataset and carries no fields. To sample fields along a segment use probeLine.
pitfalls: Coordinates use the dataset coordinate system. A line inside the bounding box can still cross solid regions or gaps.
Resolution is the number of intervals, so a line with resolution 20 has 21 points.

foam.explanation: Curated OpenFOAM reader: opens a case through its .foam marker file and outputs a multiblock dataset whose blocks are the selected mesh regions (internalMesh volume cells, patch/<name> boundaries) carrying the selected cell fields, with one time step per stored time directory. Schemaxis defaults read a decomposed case (processor* folders), only internalMesh, and keep the 0 directory; other reader settings keep ParaView's defaults, which also create point data interpolated from the cell fields. Use pvOpenFOAMReader for point or Lagrangian fields, zones, label/scalar size or the other native options.

examples.purpose: Plan one explicit time; execution requires a real CFD case. Inspect available times before choosing them.

pitfalls: caseType defaults to Decomposed Case in Schemaxis (ParaView's own default is Reconstructed Case); for a serial or reconstructed case set Reconstructed Case, otherwise the reader finds no data.
Boundary patches are loaded only when listed in regions as patch/<name>.
Pick stored times with the document's times selection using this node as the source.

readSurface.explanation: Reads one VTK XML polydata file (.vtp): polygonal surfaces, lines and vertices with point and cell arrays, such as extracted boundaries, slices or streamlines saved earlier. Use it to reopen surface artifacts, for instance in a later workflow that renders or measures them. Use readParallelPolyData for partitioned .pvtp output and readUnstructuredGrid for volume meshes.
pitfalls: Only one file is read; reopen a time series through its .pvd collection with pvPVDReader, or use pvXMLPolyDataReader with several files.

calculator.explanation: Evaluates a ParaView Calculator expression at every point or cell and adds the result as a new array named by result, e.g. velocity magnitude mag(U) or a non-dimensional group. The output is the input dataset type with one more array of the chosen association; existing arrays and geometry are unchanged. Use pvCalculator for coordinate results, other result types or table data.
pitfalls: The expression language is ParaView's parser (ExprTk syntax), not Python and not a Schemaxis $calc expression.
An expression can only use arrays of the selected association; point and cell arrays cannot be mixed, and nothing is interpolated between them.
Invalid results (e.g. sqrt of a negative) are replaced by 0 under ParaView's defaults, which can hide errors.

slice.explanation: Cuts the input with one infinite plane through origin, perpendicular to normal, and returns polygonal data: a surface from a volume mesh, lines from a surface. Point arrays are interpolated onto the cut and cell arrays are copied from the cell each polygon came from, so cell-centred CFD fields appear piecewise constant. Use it for cross-sections of 3-D fields; use clip to keep one side of a volume, contour for an isosurface, probeLine for a 1-D profile, and pvSlice for several parallel offsets or other cut shapes.
sources: ParaView 5.13.3 VTKExtensions/FiltersGeneral/vtkPVMetaSliceDataSet.cxx:76-87 (separate implicit functions per input kind)
pitfalls: origin defaults to [0, 0, 0], not to the centre of your data as in the ParaView GUI. A plane that misses the data gives empty geometry, which Schemaxis reports as EMPTY_GEOMETRY; set origin inside the dataset bounds.

Hyper tree grid input is refused with INPUT_TRAIT_MISMATCH (recovery: use pvSlice): this operation sets only ParaView's SliceType, whereas a hyper tree grid is cut by the separate HyperTreeGridImplicitFunction, so origin and normal would have no effect on it.

Native acceptance (examples/schemaxis/acceptance.py) checks that slices lie on the requested plane and that integrals over a wavelet slice match analytic values; crinkle output and real CFD meshes are not separately checked.

examples.purpose: Extract a plane through an analytic wavelet.

contour.explanation: Extracts isosurfaces (3-D input) or isolines (2-D input) where a point-centred scalar field equals each of the given values, and outputs them as polydata; several values give several surfaces in one output. Use it for level sets such as a temperature front or a Q-criterion vortex surface. By Schemaxis default the output carries normals and the contour value as an array, but no gradients. Use pvContour for the full native settings.
pitfalls: The scalar must be point data; for cell arrays run cellToPoint first.
Values outside the field's range produce an empty output without an error.

cellToPoint.explanation: Interpolates cell-centred arrays to mesh points: each point receives the average of the cells that use it, producing point fields for stream tracing, contours and smooth colouring. The mesh is unchanged. Averaging smooths sharp cell-to-cell changes and blurs discontinuities such as shocks or material interfaces. Use pointToCell for the reverse.
pitfalls: Averages are unweighted across neighbouring cells, so values at boundaries between very different cells are not conservative.
With passCellData true (Schemaxis default) the output carries both versions of each array; select the association explicitly downstream.

pointToCell.explanation: Averages point arrays onto cells: each cell receives the unweighted mean of its points' values. The mesh is unchanged; only the array association changes. Use it when a later operation, a threshold or an integration needs cell data, or to compare with cell-centred solver output. Use cellToPoint for the reverse.
pitfalls: Averaging over cell points smooths peaks; the cell values are not exact cell integrals.
With passPointData true (Schemaxis default) both versions of each array remain; select the association explicitly downstream.

extractBlock.explanation: Extracts selected blocks from a composite dataset (multiblock, partitioned dataset collection or AMR), such as the internalMesh or individual patches of an OpenFOAM case read by foam. Blocks are chosen by selectors, path expressions over the input's block hierarchy such as "/Root/internalMesh" or "//inlet". The output keeps the composite type with only the selected blocks (overlapping AMR becomes a partitioned dataset collection). Use merge afterwards when one dataset is needed; pvExtractBlock also exposes the assembly choice.
pitfalls: Selectors that match nothing give an empty composite rather than an error; check names in the input hierarchy (Studio lists them).
Only blocks that the reader loaded can be extracted; enable the patches in the reader options first.

group.explanation: Combines several input nodes into one multiblock (composite) dataset, one block per input in connection order, without changing the data. Use it to process, colour or export several parts together while keeping them distinct; use append or merge when you need a single mesh.
pitfalls: Filters that need a non-composite input will not accept the grouped result; merge it first.

merge.explanation: Merges every leaf dataset of a composite input (multiblock or partitioned data, e.g. the regions and patches from foam) into one unstructured grid, ParaView's default output type. Use it before operations or exports that need a single non-composite dataset. Point merging (on by Schemaxis default) fuses exactly coincident points at block interfaces so the result is connected. Use pvMergeBlocks for polydata output, a merge tolerance or partition-only merging, and append to combine separate nodes.
pitfalls: Block identity and names are lost; use extractBlock first if only some blocks should be merged.
Arrays that are missing on some blocks may be absent or incomplete after merging; check the output arrays.

surface.explanation: Extracts the outer boundary surface of any dataset as polygonal data: the exterior faces of volume cells plus any 2-D, line and vertex cells already present. Use it to turn a volume mesh into a surface for rendering, normals, featureEdges, decimate or surface export, or to see the whole boundary of a CFD domain (walls, inlets and outlets together). Cell arrays are copied from the adjacent cell to each face and point arrays are passed; nothing is interpolated.
pitfalls: Interior faces are removed, so use slice or clip to see inside. Composite data is surfaced block by block, so faces between blocks remain.
Cell values on the surface are those of the adjacent volume cell, not boundary-condition values; for OpenFOAM patch values select the patch regions in foam instead.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on point data derived from the wavelet; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

normals.explanation: Computes point normals of a polygonal surface by averaging the normals of adjacent polygons, for smooth shading and for operations that need normals (warping along normals, glyphs). With splitting, points on edges sharper than featureAngle are duplicated so each side keeps its own normal; consistency reorders polygons so neighbours agree. Output is polydata with a Normals point array.
sources: ParaView 5.13.3 Remoting/Application/Resources/filters_filtersparallel.xml:1186-1190,1319-1327: filters/SurfaceNormals (vtkPPolyDataNormals); the former PolyDataNormals name is a deprecated alias of the same class, so this operation binds SurfaceNormals
pitfalls: Consistent orientation does not make normals point outward; check their direction, since flipping is not exposed by this operation.
Schemaxis turns splitting off by default (ParaView's own default is on), so sharp edges are shaded smoothly unless you enable it.
Input must be polygonal; extract the surface of a volume mesh first (surface).

reflect.explanation: Mirrors the input across an axis-aligned plane and outputs an unstructured grid (a composite input gives a multiblock of unstructured grids) holding the mirrored copy, plus the original when copyInput is true. Use it to rebuild a full model from a half- or quarter-symmetry simulation, or to mirror a part for display. The plane is x, y or z = centre (Schemaxis default plane X at 0) or one face of the input's bounding box (X Min to Z Max). Vector and tensor arrays such as velocity are mirrored with the geometry because ParaView's FlipAllInputArrays stays at its default (on); scalars are copied unchanged.
pitfalls: The two halves are appended, not merged: points on the mirror plane are duplicated and the halves are not connected. Run cleanGrid afterwards when connectivity matters, e.g. before surface, connectivity or point-based gradients.
Image data, rectilinear and structured grids become an unstructured grid, which can need much more memory than the input.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a sphere with the default options; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

streamTracer.explanation: Integrates streamlines of a steady vector field from the points of a separate seed dataset and returns polygonal data made of polylines. Connect the flow dataset to input and any point-producing node (line, sphere, a slice) to seed; every seed point starts a trace. Input point arrays are interpolated onto the lines and ParaView adds IntegrationTime, Vorticity, Rotation and AngularVelocity point arrays and a ReasonForTermination cell array. Point vectors are interpolated along the trace. A cell vector array (association CELLS) is traced as constant within each cell, but ParaView's input domain also requires some three-component point array on the input, so a cell-only input fails INPUT_DOMAIN_MISMATCH at update. Convert cell-centred CFD velocity with cellToPoint for the usual smooth traces. The integrator stays at ParaView's Runge-Kutta 4-5 with step lengths in cell lengths. Use pvStreamTracerWithCustomSource to change the integrator, step unit or terminal speed, and pvStreamTracer for ParaView's built-in seed shapes.
sources: ParaView 5.13.3 VTK/Filters/FlowPaths/vtkAbstractInterpolatedVelocityField.cxx:244-258 (cell vectors read by cell id)
pitfalls: These are instantaneous streamlines at the selected time, not pathlines or particle tracks through changing timesteps.
maximumLength (Schemaxis default 20) is an absolute arc length in dataset units, not a fraction of the domain; scale it to your geometry, or lines in a large domain stop early.

Empty or truncated lines usually mean seeds outside the flow cells, the wrong vector array, or speed below ParaView's terminal speed (1e-12). ReasonForTermination tells why each line stopped: 1 left the domain, 4 maximum length, 5 maximum steps, 6 terminal speed.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, tracing a uniform analytic velocity from a line of seeds; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

tube.explanation: Builds a polygonal tube of constant radius around each line or polyline of polygonal input, typically streamlines from streamTracer, so that thin lines become visible shaded geometry in images and exports. The output is vtkPolyData, and input point arrays are carried onto the tube surface so it can be coloured by the same fields. Schemaxis assigns radius 0.1, 12 sides and capped ends; ParaView's radius variation stays off, so use pvTube for tubes whose radius follows a scalar or vector.
pitfalls: radius is an absolute length in dataset units: 0.1 vanishes on a 100 m domain and swamps a 1 mm one. ParaView's GUI starts from 1% of the input extent, a reasonable first choice.
Lines with repeated consecutive points are not tubed; run clean first if segments are missing.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on streamlines of a uniform analytic field; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

clip.explanation: Cuts the input with a plane through origin with normal normal and keeps one side, returning an unstructured grid of whole and cut cells (dimension is kept, unlike slice). With the Schemaxis default invert false the kept half is the side the normal points into; true keeps the opposite side. Use it to open a volume for viewing interior fields; use pvClip for box, sphere, cylinder or scalar clips and for crinkle (whole-cell) clipping.
pitfalls: ParaView's own Clip starts with Invert on (keeping the side opposite the normal); Schemaxis sets invert false by default, so results can be mirrored relative to a ParaView GUI session.
Clipping structured data produces an unstructured grid, which can use much more memory.

threshold.explanation: Keeps the cells of a mesh whose selected point or cell scalar lies inside the inclusive range [lower, upper], producing an unstructured grid. Schemaxis fixes ParaView's ThresholdMethod to Between, requires all three options, checks that lower does not exceed upper and that the named array exists with the stated association. Use it to isolate a region such as hot gas or a recirculation zone; use pvThreshold for inverted, one-sided or component-wise tests.
pitfalls: For point arrays ParaView's AllScalars default (true) applies: a cell is kept only if all of its points are in range, which shrinks the region compared with a cell-array threshold.
Cells are kept whole, so the boundary is stepped; use contour or clip for a smooth iso-boundary.

integrate.explanation: Integrates all point and cell arrays over the input's cells and computes the total length, area or volume, producing a one-point unstructured grid with one integrated value per array. Only cells of the highest dimension present are used (a volume mesh ignores its faces) and vertex cells are not integrated. With divideByVolume the cell-data integrals are divided by the total size, giving size-weighted means. Use it for totals such as mass or force and for mean values; results carry the array units times length, area or volume.
pitfalls: Point-data results are never divided; for a point-field mean divide by the size array yourself or convert to cell data first.
Integrating a vector gives componentwise integrals, not a flux; compute the normal component with a calculator first.

probeLine.explanation: Samples the input's point and cell arrays along the segment from start to end (Plot Over Line), interpolating within cells, and outputs a polyline with the sampled arrays plus arc_length and vtkValidPointMask (1 where a sample lies inside the data). Use it for spatial profiles, e.g. velocity across a channel. ParaView's XML default sampling pattern is uniform, for which resolution (Schemaxis default 100) is the number of intervals.
pitfalls: Samples outside the mesh have vtkValidPointMask 0 and placeholder values; mask them before plotting or measuring.
Sampling behaviour follows the native PlotOverLine settings; resolution controls the uniform-sampling mode.

outline.explanation: Produces the 12 edges of the input's axis-aligned bounding box as polydata lines. Use it as a context frame in scenes or to check a dataset's extent; it carries no field data.
pitfalls: The box is axis-aligned, so it can be much larger than a rotated or thin object.

warpVector.explanation: Moves every point by scale times a three-component point vector (new position = point + scale x vector), typically to show a structural displacement field or exaggerate a deformation mode. The output keeps the input type (image data and rectilinear grids become structured grids) and carries all arrays. With scale 1 and a displacement in the same length units as the coordinates the result is the true deformed shape; warping by a velocity is only a visual distortion.
pitfalls: The displacement must be in the coordinate units: a displacement in millimetres on a mesh in metres needs scale 0.001 for the true shape.
Large scales can fold or invert cells; do not compute volumes or mesh quality on an exaggerated warp.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a wavelet with a uniform vector field and scale 0.25; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

warpScalar.explanation: Displaces each point along a direction by scale times a point scalar (new position = point + scale x value x direction), turning a field on a flat surface into a relief or carpet plot, or moving a surface by a normal displacement. With useNormal true (Schemaxis default) every point moves along the same normal (default z+); with useNormal false the input's point normals are used when present. The output keeps the input type, except that image data and rectilinear grids become a structured grid; all arrays are carried along.
pitfalls: The warp distance is in dataset units: choose scale so that the field range times scale is a modest fraction of the geometry size, otherwise the relief dwarfs or hides the shape.
Schemaxis normalizes normal, so its length does not change the displacement; express any magnification through scale.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a planar slice with a linear field; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

shrink.explanation: Moves the points of every cell towards that cell's centroid (the average of its points) so that cells separate from their neighbours, and outputs an unstructured grid in which no point is shared between cells. It is a mesh-inspection aid that reveals cell shapes, sizes and gaps inside a volume or surface mesh; point and cell arrays travel with the cells. factor is the fraction of each cell's size kept (Schemaxis default 0.8; ParaView's own default is 0.5).
pitfalls: Every shared point is duplicated once per cell, so point count and memory grow several-fold on volume meshes; shrink a slice, surface or extracted subset of a large mesh instead.
Do not measure or integrate the result: shrinking scales each cell's area by factor squared and its volume by factor cubed.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a sphere with the default factor; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

clean.explanation: Cleans polygonal data: merges duplicate points within a tolerance, removes unused points and turns degenerate cells into lower-dimensional ones (a triangle with two merged points becomes a line). Output is polydata. Use it after appendGeometry or on surfaces with duplicated vertices to get a connected surface for normals, curvature, connectivity or decimation. For other dataset types use cleanGrid.
pitfalls: A large tolerance collapses small features and can change topology; keep it well below the smallest edge length.

cleanGrid.explanation: Converts any dataset into an unstructured grid and merges coincident points (exactly coincident at the Schemaxis default tolerance 0), optionally removing points used by no cell (Schemaxis default true). Use it to obtain an unstructured grid for operations that need one, or to stitch appended parts. Use clean when the input is polydata and polydata output is wanted.
pitfalls: Structured inputs lose their implicit structure and grow in memory once converted.

delaunay3D.explanation: Builds a 3-D Delaunay tetrahedralization of the input points (any point set) and outputs an unstructured grid of tetrahedra filling their convex hull. A positive alpha (Schemaxis default 0) produces an alpha shape: only tetrahedra whose circumsphere radius is at most alpha, plus qualifying triangles, are kept, which recovers concave shapes from point clouds. Use it to mesh scattered 3-D samples for interpolation or volume estimates; use delaunay2D for surface-like sets and pvDelaunay3D to choose which alpha cell types are output.
pitfalls: Output grows quickly and ParaView warns that Delaunay 3D can exhaust memory; thin large point sets first.
Points on a regular lattice are degenerate: the result depends on point order, and nearly coplanar points produce sliver tetrahedra.

delaunay2D.explanation: Builds a 2-D Delaunay triangulation of the input points (any point set, e.g. a point cloud or the points of a mesh; input cells are ignored) and outputs polydata triangles. Triangulation is done in the x-y plane: z is ignored for connectivity but kept on the points, so it suits height fields and nearly planar sets aligned with x-y. With alpha 0 (Schemaxis default) every triangle of the convex hull is kept; a positive alpha keeps only triangles whose circumcircle radius is at most alpha, carving concave outlines and gaps. Use pvDelaunay2D for a best-fitting plane, and delaunay3D for tetrahedra.
pitfalls: Points on a plane not parallel to x-y (e.g. a vertical wall) triangulate badly or collapse; transform them first or use pvDelaunay2D with ProjectionPlaneMode Best-Fitting Plane.
Points closer than tolerance (a fraction of the bounding-box diagonal) are discarded as duplicates.

elevation.explanation: Adds a point scalar array named Elevation: each point is projected onto the line from lowPoint to highPoint and the position along that line is mapped linearly onto range, clamped at both ends. Use it to colour by height or depth along any direction, or as a synthetic field for testing. Schemaxis assigns its defaults (z from -1 to 1 mapped to 0 to 1), so set the points to your data's extent.
pitfalls: Points beyond either end point all receive the end value, so a line shorter than the data flattens the field outside it.

gradient.explanation: Estimates the spatial gradient of a point or cell array and stores it as a new array on the same mesh: 3 components for a scalar, 9 (row-major d(component)/d(x, y, z)) for a 3-component vector. Optionally adds divergence, vorticity and the Q-criterion of a vector field, e.g. for vortex identification. Unstructured meshes use cell derivatives, structured ones central differences. Use pvGradient for the full native settings and other output names.
pitfalls: Divergence, vorticity and Q-criterion need a 3-component array; they fail or are skipped for scalars.
Derivatives are in field units per dataset length unit; no unit conversion is applied.

cellSize.explanation: Adds cell-data arrays holding the size of each cell: Length for 1-D cells (lines, polylines), Area for 2-D cells (triangles, quads, polygons) and Volume for 3-D cells, all in dataset coordinate units (length, length squared, length cubed). Cells of a dimension that is not computed get 0 in that array. Use it for cell volumes or face areas, e.g. to weight cell values or check mesh resolution; with sum enabled the totals are also stored as field data. pvCellSize exposes the same filter with every native setting, including the vertex count and array names; pvMeshQuality rates cell shape instead of size.
pitfalls: Each array is filled for every cell, so a mixed mesh shows 0 in Volume for its faces and 0 in Area for its volume cells; filter by cell type before taking statistics.
Polygon areas are computed by a fan triangulation that is exact only for convex planar polygons.

connectivity.explanation: Labels the connected regions of the input (cells linked through shared points) and keeps all regions, the largest one (most cells) or the one closest to a point; output is an unstructured grid. With colourRegions (Schemaxis default true) a RegionId array identifies each region. Use it to separate disjoint bodies, drop small fragments or isolate the part near a location.
pitfalls: Connectivity is topological: parts that touch only geometrically, with duplicate points, count as separate regions; run clean or cleanGrid first.

decimate.explanation: Reduces the triangle count of a polygonal surface by a target fraction (Schemaxis default 0.5) with vtkDecimatePro, trying to preserve shape; preserveTopology (Schemaxis default true) prevents holes and splits at the cost of possibly missing the target. Use it to lighten large surfaces for rendering or export. Input must be triangles; run triangulate first if other polygons are present.
pitfalls: Small features and sharp detail are lost first; compare with the original before measuring on the result.

smooth.explanation: Applies Laplacian smoothing to a polygonal surface: each iteration moves every point a small step towards the average of its connected neighbours. The output is polygonal data with the same points and connectivity at smoother positions, and arrays are passed unchanged. Use it to reduce faceting or noise on scanned, marching-cubes or STL surfaces before rendering or curvature. Input must be vtkPolyData; run surface first on volume meshes.
pitfalls: Laplacian smoothing shrinks surfaces and rounds sharp features; compare volumes or key dimensions with the input before measuring the result.
VTK's relaxation factor (0.01) is not exposed, so 20 iterations move points only slightly; raise iterations for stronger smoothing.
Feature edges are not protected and open boundaries are smoothed too (VTK defaults: feature-edge smoothing off, boundary smoothing on); neither smooth nor pvSmooth exposes these switches.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a sphere with the default options; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

triangulate.explanation: Converts polygonal data so that every polygon and triangle strip becomes triangles and polylines become single line segments; vertices are kept. The output is vtkPolyData on the same points, with cell values copied from each parent cell. Use it before operations or exports that need triangles, such as decimate or STL output. It accepts only polygonal input: run surface first for volume data, or use pvTetrahedralize to split volume cells into tetrahedra.
pitfalls: The cell count grows (a quadrilateral becomes two triangles) and cell values are repeated on each piece, so per-cell counts and cell-based statistics change, while point data is unaffected.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a wavelet slice; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

append.explanation: Combines the meshes of several input nodes (any dataset types, non-composite) into one unstructured grid, ParaView 5.13.3's default output type for Append Datasets. Points are not merged and only point and cell arrays present on every input are kept. Use it to treat parts as one dataset for a filter or export; use appendGeometry for surfaces, group to keep inputs as separate blocks, and merge for the blocks of one composite node.
pitfalls: Arrays missing on any input are dropped; make array names consistent across inputs first.
Coincident points at part interfaces stay duplicated; follow with cleanGrid to merge them.

appendGeometry.explanation: Appends several polygonal (vtkPolyData) inputs, such as surfaces, lines or point clouds, into one polydata without merging points. Only point and cell arrays common to all inputs survive. Use it to combine surface parts for a joint export or surface filter; use append for mixed dataset types.
pitfalls: Shared edges between parts keep duplicate points; run clean afterwards for a connected surface (needed for consistent normals or connectivity).

transform.explanation: Applies a linear transform to the point coordinates: scale, then rotation, then translation, all about the coordinate origin [0, 0, 0]. Vectors and normals are transformed with the geometry (every three-component array while allVectors is true). Polygonal, unstructured and structured grids keep their type; image data and rectilinear grids become an explicit-point dataset. Use it to position, orient or rescale geometry, e.g. scale [0.001, 0.001, 0.001] to convert millimetre coordinates to metres.
pitfalls: Rotation and scaling act about the origin, not the dataset centre, so an object away from the origin also moves. Translate it to the origin first, or use pvTransform with RotateAroundOriginTransform.
Transformed vector arrays are rotated and scaled too: a millimetre-to-metre scale also multiplies velocity-like vectors by 0.001. Field values are never unit-converted.

Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, translating a sphere by [1, 2, 3]; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

resample.explanation: Samples the arrays of the input node (port input, native SourceDataArrays) at the points of the mesh node (port mesh, native DestinationMesh). The result has the mesh's geometry with the input's point and cell values interpolated to its points and a vtkValidPointMask array; with passPointArrays (Schemaxis default true) the mesh's own point arrays are kept too. Use it to compare or combine results on a common mesh, e.g. map a CFD field onto a measurement or structural mesh; pvResampleWithDataset exposes the remaining native settings.
pitfalls: The ports are easily swapped: input supplies the values, mesh supplies the geometry.
Mesh points outside the input get vtkValidPointMask 0 and unusable values; threshold on the mask before statistics.

edges.explanation: Extracts every edge of every cell as a line cell, giving a wireframe polydata of the whole mesh, including interior edges of volume cells. Each shared edge appears once and receives the cell data of the lowest-numbered cell using it. Use it to show or export mesh structure or to measure edge lengths; use featureEdges for only boundary or sharp edges of a surface, and run surface first if only the outer skin's edges are wanted.
pitfalls: On volume meshes the output holds all interior edges and can be several times larger than the input; ParaView warns about memory for structured inputs.

featureEdges.explanation: Extracts edges of a polygonal surface as line cells (polydata): boundary edges (used by one polygon), feature edges (between two polygons whose normals differ by more than angle), non-manifold edges (shared by three or more polygons) and optionally manifold edges. With the Schemaxis defaults (boundary, feature and non-manifold on, manifold off, 30°) it outlines a CAD or CFD surface's creases, open boundaries and T-junctions. Input must be polydata; run surface first on volume meshes. Use edges for every cell edge.
pitfalls: Feature detection uses polygon normals, so inconsistently oriented polygons create spurious feature edges; run normals with consistency first.
Unmerged duplicate points make every polygon edge a boundary edge; run clean first.

temporalStatistics.explanation: Computes, for every point and cell array of a time-dependent input, its average, minimum, maximum and population standard deviation over all input time steps, which the filter requests itself. The output has the input's type and geometry, no time, and arrays named <name>_average, <name>_minimum, <name>_maximum and <name>_stddev (other arrays are not kept). Every step is weighted equally regardless of time spacing, so this is not a time integral. Schemaxis enables all four statistics by default; use pvTemporalStatistics only if you want the generated binding with native option names.
pitfalls: Unequal time steps bias the average; resample time first if the spacing varies.
Every time step is read and processed, which can take long on large series; restrict the input time range first.
The mesh must keep the same points and cells over time; on changing meshes the statistics are meaningless.

cone.explanation: Creates a polygonal cone surface of given height and base radius. Its centre is the midpoint of the axis, the axis follows direction, and the apex lies on the direction side; resolution sets the number of facets around the axis and capping closes the base. Use it as a marker, glyph or simple test geometry; coordinates are in the units of the data it is shown with.
pitfalls: centre is not the centre of the base: the base lies height/2 behind it and the apex height/2 ahead along direction.

cylinder.explanation: Creates a polygonal cylinder surface of given radius and height, centred on centre with its axis parallel to y, including point normals and texture coordinates. resolution sets the facets around the axis and capping closes both ends. There is no orientation setting: follow it with transform to rotate the cylinder.
pitfalls: The axis is always along y before any transform; a cylinder meant along z needs a 90-degree rotation about x.

plane.explanation: Creates a flat parallelogram (polydata) with one corner at origin and edges running to point1 and point2, subdivided into xResolution × yResolution quadrilaterals. Use it as a probe or seed surface, for example for resampling or streamline seeds, or as test geometry. The Schemaxis defaults give a 2 × 2 square in the XY plane centred at the origin, with 10 × 10 cells.
pitfalls: point1 and point2 must not be collinear with origin, or the plane is degenerate.

disk.explanation: Creates a flat annulus (polydata) centred at the origin in the XY plane, with inner and outer radius and radial and circumferential resolution; set innerRadius to 0 for a full disc. Use it as a seed or probe surface, a marker or test geometry, and place it with transform.
pitfalls: Schemaxis requires innerRadius not to exceed outerRadius.

readUnstructuredGrid.explanation: Reads one VTK XML unstructured grid file (.vtu) into vtkUnstructuredGrid, with any mix of cell types (tetrahedra, hexahedra, wedges, polyhedra) and all point and cell arrays. Use it to reopen volume meshes exported by Schemaxis, Gmsh or a solver; it is the reader covered by Schemaxis's reader fixture. Use pvXMLUnstructuredGridReader when you need array selection or a file series, and readParallelUnstructuredGrid for .pvtu output.
pitfalls: Coordinates are in whatever unit the writer used; nothing is converted.

readParallelPolyData.explanation: Reads a partitioned VTK XML polydata dataset: the .pvtp summary file plus the per-piece .vtp files it lists, typically written by an MPI run. The pieces are combined into polydata (surfaces, lines, vertices) with their point and cell arrays. Use it to reopen distributed surface output, including Schemaxis's own native parallel geometry; in Schemaxis MPI runs it is one of the operations qualified for distributed reading. Use readSurface for a single .vtp file.
pitfalls: The .pvtp summary refers to its piece files by relative path; move them together.
Pieces may share boundary points; run clean before connectivity or point-count checks.

readParallelUnstructuredGrid.explanation: Reads a partitioned VTK XML unstructured grid: the .pvtu summary file plus the per-piece .vtu files it lists, typically written by an MPI run. The result is an unstructured grid with the point and cell arrays of all pieces. Use it to reopen distributed volume output, including Schemaxis's native parallel geometry (examples/schemaxis/foam-native-parallel.json); it is in Schemaxis's MPI-qualified operation list. Use readUnstructuredGrid for a single .vtu file.
pitfalls: The .pvtu summary refers to its piece files by relative path; move them together.
Ghost cells or duplicated interface points between pieces can affect counts and integrals; check vtkGhostType or clean the grid when exact counts matter.

readImageData.explanation: Reads one VTK XML image data file (.vti) into vtkImageData: a uniform grid defined by extent, origin and spacing, with point and cell arrays. Use it for voxel or pixel data such as sampled volumes, resampled CFD fields or images exported by ParaView; the result suits volume rendering, contouring and image filters. For curvilinear or irregular meshes use readStructuredGrid or readUnstructuredGrid.
pitfalls: Every point and cell array is read; on large volumes use the generated pvXMLImageDataReader binding, which can select arrays.
Only one file is read; for a time series use a .pvd collection (pvPVDReader) or the generated pvXMLImageDataReader binding.

readStructuredGrid.explanation: Reads one VTK XML structured grid file (.vts) into vtkStructuredGrid: a curvilinear i-j-k grid with explicit point coordinates and implicit hexahedral (or quadrilateral) connectivity. Use it for body-fitted structured meshes, e.g. multi-block CFD grids exported block by block. For axis-aligned grids use readRectilinearGrid or readImageData; for arbitrary cells use readUnstructuredGrid.
pitfalls: Coordinates are in whatever unit the writer used; nothing is converted.
Every array is read; use the generated pvXMLStructuredGridReader binding to select arrays on large grids.

readRectilinearGrid.explanation: Reads one VTK XML rectilinear grid file (.vtr) into vtkRectilinearGrid: an axis-aligned structured grid whose x, y and z coordinates are given by three independent (possibly non-uniform) coordinate arrays. Use it for tensor-product meshes with graded spacing, e.g. stretched finite-difference grids. For uniform spacing readImageData is the lighter equivalent; for curved structured meshes use readStructuredGrid.
pitfalls: Some image filters require vtkImageData; resample to an image when a downstream operation rejects rectilinear input.

readMultiBlock.explanation: Reads a VTK XML multiblock file (.vtm, or the older .vtmb): a small index file that names the serial VTK XML files of each block and nests them in a block hierarchy. The output is a vtkMultiBlockDataSet whose leaves may mix datasets of different types. Use it to reopen composite results such as a multi-region case saved by ParaView or Schemaxis; follow it with extractBlock to pick blocks or merge to combine them into one dataset.
pitfalls: Keep the .vtm file together with its block-file folder; the index refers to the block files by relative path.
Many filters run per block; merge the blocks first when an operation must see one connected dataset.

readSTL.explanation: Reads one ASCII or binary STL file into polydata made of triangles. STL stores only triangle geometry, with no units or field arrays, so coordinates are in whatever unit the exporting CAD tool used. Use it for CAD or scanned surfaces to render, clip against, or probe onto; add normals for smooth shading. Schemaxis reads exactly one file (no file series).
pitfalls: Check the coordinate unit (millimetres versus metres) against the simulation data before combining them; nothing is converted.

readPLY.explanation: Curated PLY reader: reads exactly one Stanford PLY file (ASCII or binary) into polydata, with vertex properties such as normals, colours or texture coordinates carried as arrays. PLY has no unit, so coordinates are in whatever unit the scanner or CAD tool used. Use it for scanned or meshed surfaces to render, clip or probe; use pvPLYReader for file series or texture settings, and readSTL for STL.
pitfalls: Check the coordinate unit (millimetres versus metres) against the simulation data before combining them; nothing is converted.

generateIds.explanation: Adds arrays holding each point's and each cell's index (zero-based ids in the input), so that later clipping, extraction or merging carries the original ids along and results can be traced back to the source mesh. The geometry and type are unchanged and existing arrays are kept; each generated id array becomes that attribute's active scalars. For hyper-tree grids cell ids are always generated, and pointIds, pointName and cellIds have no effect.
sources: ParaView 5.13.3 VTK/Filters/Core/vtkGenerateIds.cxx:27-66 (shallow copy keeps input arrays; hyper-tree-grid branch generates cell ids only)
pitfalls: Ids are indices in this node's input, not solver-native ids; apply the operation before filters that renumber points or cells.

passArrays.explanation: Keeps only the named point, cell and field arrays of the input and removes every other array of those associations; geometry and topology are unchanged (shallow copy, so it is cheap). Use it to slim a dataset before export or publication, or to drop arrays that would confuse later steps. Each list has the Schemaxis default [], and an empty list keeps none of that association's arrays. Use pvPassArrays when vertex, edge or row (table) arrays also need selecting.
pitfalls: Listing only pointArrays removes every cell and field array, because the other lists default to []; list the arrays you need in each association.
Names are matched exactly; a misspelt name keeps nothing and the array disappears.
Ghost-cell arrays (vtkGhostType) are kept unless explicitly deselected.

curvature.explanation: Computes per-point curvature of a polygonal surface (Gaussian or mean, the two curvature types ParaView 5.13.3 offers) as a point array such as Mean_Curvature or Gauss_Curvature. Use it to locate ridges, valleys or highly curved regions on CAD or scanned surfaces. Mean curvature is in inverse length units and Gaussian in inverse length squared; both are noisy on coarse or irregular triangulations. The mean-curvature sign assumes outward normals.
pitfalls: type accepts only Gaussian or Mean, the entries of ParaView 5.13.3's Curvature enumeration (filters_filtersgeneral.xml:445-485); maximum and minimum principal curvature are not available and any other value is rejected at planning.
If convex regions show negative mean curvature, the normals point inward; set invertMean.

extractSubset.explanation: Extracts a volume of interest from structured data (image data, rectilinear or structured grid) by an IJK point-index range, optionally keeping every n-th index. The output keeps the input's structured type, so it stays compact and works with structured filters. Use it to crop a structured block or image by index; use a clip for geometric cuts or unstructured meshes.
pitfalls: Indices are in the input's extent space, which need not start at 0; inspect the input extent before choosing the range.

pvADIOS2CoreImageReader.explanation: Reads variables from an ADIOS2 BP file or BP4/BP5 directory as arrays on a uniform image (vtkImageData). One variable (Image Dimension) defines the image size; each selected variable becomes a point or cell array according to its shape, and an optional variable supplies the time values. Use it for simulation codes that write plain multi-dimensional arrays through ADIOS2; use pvADIOS2VTXReader when the file embeds a VTK schema and pvFidesReader when it follows a Fides data model.
pitfalls: Arrays whose shape matches neither the point nor the cell dimensions of the chosen dimension variable cannot be placed on the image; pick the dimension variable that matches the fields you need.
Schemaxis generates this reader binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check with a sample file of this format.

pvADIOS2VTXReader.explanation: Reads an ADIOS2 BP file or BP4 directory that embeds a VTK XML schema (VTX), either as a BP attribute or as a vtk.xml subfile, describing image data (vti) or unstructured grid (vtu) content; the output is that dataset, with time steps from the BP steps. It is a distributed reader. Choose it for codes that write VTX-annotated ADIOS2 output (e.g. via the VTX schema), and pvADIOS2CoreImageReader or pvFidesReader for other ADIOS2 layouts.
pitfalls: Files without the embedded VTK schema cannot be interpreted by this reader.
Schemaxis generates this reader binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check with a sample file of this format.

pvAMRConnectivity.explanation: Fragment identification on non-overlapping AMR material data (such as CTH output from pvSpyPlotReader): for each selected volume-fraction cell array it labels connected regions of cells whose value exceeds VolumeFractionValue, including across block and level boundaries when ResolveBlocks is on, and adds a cell array RegionId-<array name>. The output is the same AMR data with these labels; pvAMRFragmentIntegration then sums fragment volumes and masses. Use pvAMRFragmentsFilter to run the whole chain in one step.
pitfalls: Unlike AMR Contour and AMR Dual Clip, this filter compares VolumeFractionValue with the stored array values without scaling by 255; with unsigned char fractions the default 0.1 therefore keeps any cell with a non-zero fraction.
Without at least one SelectMaterialArrays entry no labels are produced.
Overlapping AMR is rejected; the input must be vtkNonOverlappingAMR.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAMRContour.explanation: AMR Contour (vtkPVAMRDualContour) extracts material interface surfaces from non-overlapping AMR volume-fraction data using the dual grid, so surfaces stay crack-free across refinement levels. For each selected cell array it outputs a block of polygonal surface at VolumeFractionValue (multiplied by 255 internally), optionally capped where the material meets the domain boundary. Use it to visualize material boundaries in CTH-style AMR data; for meshes or image data use contour.
pitfalls: Volume fractions are expected as unsigned char 0-255 (as the Spy Plot reader produces by default); VolumeFractionValue is a fraction of 1 and is multiplied by 255, so 0.5 means a stored value of 127.5.
Nothing is produced until at least one SelectMaterialArrays entry is given.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAMRDualClip.explanation: AMR Dual Clip (vtkPVAMRDualClip) clips non-overlapping AMR volume-fraction data with the dual grid and outputs, per selected material array, an unstructured grid of tetrahedra covering the region where the fraction exceeds VolumeFractionValue (multiplied by 255 internally). Level transitions are handled and interior tetrahedra can be decimated to keep the mesh small. Use it to get a volumetric mesh of a material region; use pvAMRContour for its surface only.
pitfalls: Volume fractions are expected as unsigned char 0-255 (as the Spy Plot reader produces by default); only unsigned char arrays are accepted here.
The native class documentation states that it does not copy attributes yet; check which arrays the clipped mesh carries before relying on them.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAMRFragmentIntegration.explanation: Integrates fragments previously labelled by pvAMRConnectivity: for each material array it reads the RegionId-<array name> cell labels and outputs a table (one block per material in a multiblock) with "Fragment ID", "Fragment Volume", "Fragment Mass" and one "Volume Weighted <name>" or "Mass Weighted <name>" column per selected array. Fragment volume is the volume fraction (0-255 scaled) times cell volume; mass is the sum of the chosen mass array. Use it for size and mass statistics of debris or droplets; pvAMRFragmentsFilter runs connectivity and integration together.
pitfalls: The input must come from pvAMRConnectivity with the same material arrays; otherwise the native filter reports that no RegionId array exists.
Give exactly one mass array per material array, in the same order; the native code pairs them by position.
Mass arrays are summed as they are, so they must hold mass per cell, not density.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAMRFragmentsFilter.explanation: One-step fragment analysis for non-overlapping AMR material data: it runs AMR connectivity (always resolving fragments across blocks), then fragment integration and optionally surface extraction, with one shared VolumeFractionValue. Output port 0 holds the fragment tables ("Fragment ID", "Fragment Volume", "Fragment Mass" and one "Volume Weighted <name>" or "Mass Weighted <name>" column per selected array) when IntegrateFragments is on; port 1 holds the fragment surfaces when ExtractSurface is on, made watertight by the AMR dual contour if UseWatertightSurface is set or by ExtractCTHPart otherwise. Select a port with {"node": id, "port": n}.
pitfalls: The shared VolumeFractionValue is used raw by the connectivity step but scaled by 255 by the contour step, so labels and surfaces can disagree slightly near the threshold.
Give one mass array per material array, in the same order.
With default settings port 1 is empty; enable ExtractSurface to get surfaces.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAMRGaussianPulseSource.explanation: Generates a small synthetic overlapping AMR dataset (vtkOverlappingAMR) with two levels: a root block of 6 × 6 (× 6) points starting at (-2, -2, 0) with spacing RootSpacing, plus two refined patches. Cell arrays are "Gaussian-Pulse" = PulseAmplitude · exp(-Σ((x - origin)/width)²) and "Centroid". Use it to test AMR pipelines and readers (compare with pvXMLUniformGridAMRReader); it is not physical data.
pitfalls: The pulse origin and width are in the same coordinates as the grid; with the default spacing 0.5 the root block spans only [-2, 0.5] in x and y, so a pulse placed far outside is invisible.
Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

pvAMReXBoxLibGridReader.explanation: Reads AMReX/BoxLib plotfiles (directories named like plt00000) into a hierarchical-box (overlapping AMR) dataset of cell-centred grid variables, levels 0 to Level. Listing several plotfile directories in FileNames makes a time series. Use it for AMReX codes such as Castro, Nyx, MAESTROeX or PeleC; use pvAMReXBoxLibParticlesReader for the particles stored in the same plotfiles.
pitfalls: Level defaults to 1, so only the two coarsest levels are loaded; raise it to see the finest data.
Each FileNames entry is a plotfile directory, not the Header file inside it.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAMReXBoxLibParticlesReader.explanation: Reads particles stored in AMReX plotfiles, producing point data (polydata blocks) with the selected particle components as point arrays; ParticleType names the particle container subdirectory inside each plotfile (ParaView default "particles"). It is a distributed reader. Several plotfile directories form a time series. Use pvAMReXBoxLibGridReader for the grid variables of the same plotfiles.
pitfalls: ParticleType must match the subdirectory name in the plotfile (e.g. DM or Tracer for some codes); a wrong name yields no particles.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvANLHaloFinder.explanation: Cosmology halo finder from the HACC CosmoTools library (vtkPANLHaloFinder). Input is an unstructured grid of particles with point arrays vx, vy, vz and id, as read by pvGenericIOReader. It links particles closer than Linkinglength (in units of the mean interparticle spacing) into friends-of-friends halos of at least FOFparticlethreshold particles. Port 0 returns the particles with fof_halo_tag (-1 outside halos), port 1 one point per halo with mass, centre of mass, mean velocity, velocity dispersion and centre, and port 2 subhalos when FindSubhalos is on.
pitfalls: Boxsize, Seedparticles and ParticleMass must match the simulation: the interparticle spacing that Linkinglength is measured in is Boxsize / Seedparticles, and the ParaView defaults are example values.
Positions must lie in [0, Boxsize); others are wrapped periodically.
Centre finding other than None can be very slow on large halos.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvANLSubhaloFinder.explanation: Runs the CosmoTools subhalo finder (vtkPANLSubhaloFinder) on halos already found by pvANLHaloFinder: the input is that filter's port 0 particles with vx, vy, vz, id and fof_halo_tag. Port 0 returns the particles with a subhalo_tag array (-1 outside subhalos) and port 1 one point per subhalo with mass, centre of mass, mean velocity and velocity dispersion. Mode chooses all halos, halos larger than SizeThreshold, or only the halo ids in HalosToProcess.
pitfalls: Feed it pvANLHaloFinder output port 0; plain particle data lack fof_halo_tag.
Use the same Boxsize, Seedparticles and ParticleMass as the halo finder.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAVSUCDReader.explanation: Reads AVS Unstructured Cell Data files (.inp, ASCII or binary) into an unstructured grid with optional point (node) and cell arrays. Several files in FileNames form a time series. Use it for meshes and results exported in AVS UCD form by FE or CFD tools.
pitfalls: Only the arrays named in the file are available; coordinates are used as written, with no unit conversion.

Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

pvAdaptiveCosmoCore.explanation: Reads LANL cosmo-format particle data that an adaptive-sampling preprocessor split into resolution levels (vtkACosmoReader, extension .cosmo). The output is a multiblock with one block per level (block 0 empty), each holding particle unstructured grids; Level chooses how many levels to load (1 is the coarsest). Use pvCosmoReader for ordinary single-resolution cosmo or Gadget files.
pitfalls: File names must follow the preprocessor pattern <base>.<process>.<levels>.cosmo; a dot elsewhere in the path, for example in a folder name, breaks this parsing.
Data sampled in parallel (process number above 0) are rejected by the reader.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAdaptiveResampleToImage.explanation: Resamples any dataset onto several image (vtkImageData) blocks, output as a vtkPartitionedDataSet: a k-d tree splits the input points into at least NumberOfImages regions (rounded up to a power of two; 0 means one per MPI process, so one in serial), and each region is sampled with SamplingDimensions points, so densely populated regions get finer spacing. Points outside the input are marked invalid, as with pvResampleToImage. Use it to obtain regular grids of unevenly distributed data for volume rendering or image analysis; use pvResampleToImage for one image over the whole domain.
pitfalls: Each block has its own spacing and origin; do not treat the blocks as one uniform grid.
The sample count is the number of blocks times the product of SamplingDimensions; 8 blocks of 64 × 64 × 64 already give about 2 million points.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAddFieldArrays.explanation: Deprecated name (since ParaView 5.13, removal planned for 5.14) of pvFieldArraysFromFile, with the same behaviour: the input passes through and the field-data arrays of a legacy VTK file (.vtk) are attached to it, to every block of a composite input. Use pvFieldArraysFromFile in new documents.
pitfalls: Documents using this id will need updating when ParaView removes the alias.
Only field data is added, never point or cell arrays.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAggregateDataset.explanation: Parallel data-movement filter: gathers the pieces of a distributed dataset onto NumberOfTargetProcesses MPI processes (ParaView default 1), leaving the other processes empty; VTK documents it for polydata and unstructured grids. Use it in MPI runs to reduce the number of pieces before writing or rendering a modest result. In a serial run there is only one process and the data pass through. Input must be a single, non-composite dataset.
pitfalls: Gathering a large dataset onto few processes can exhaust their memory.
Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAlignImageOrigins.explanation: Gives every image block of a composite (multiblock or partitioned) image dataset the same origin and rewrites each block's extent relative to it, so blocks that are parts of one image share a global index space and extent-based operations such as extractSubset behave consistently across blocks. All images must have the same spacing; the shared origin is the minimum corner of all blocks, shifted so that corner gets index MinimumExtent. Point positions do not change.
pitfalls: Blocks with different spacing cannot be aligned; ParaView reports an error.
Blocks whose origins are not offset by whole multiples of the spacing cannot keep their positions; the native code reports them as misaligned.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAngularPeriodicFilter.explanation: Rebuilds a full rotor or periodic set of sectors from a computed sector: selected blocks are copied and rotated about an axis (X, Y or Z through Center) by multiples of an angle, rotating point coordinates and 3- and 9-component arrays (vectors and tensors) consistently. Each selected leaf becomes a multipiece of rotated copies, the first being the original; with IterationMode Maximum (ParaView default) there are round(360 / angle) copies, otherwise NumberOfPeriods. The angle is RotationAngle in degrees (default 10) or read in radians from a field array. VTK supports polydata, structured and unstructured grid leaves.
pitfalls: For multiblock input only blocks listed in BlockIndices are rotated; with none listed the output is an unchanged copy. A single non-composite dataset is always processed.
Rotated arrays are computed on the fly by default (ComputeRotationsOnTheFly), saving memory but costing time at every access.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAnimateModes.explanation: Turns modal-analysis results, where each 'time step' of the input (e.g. Exodus) is really a mode shape, into a vibration animation: ModeShape (1-based) picks the mode, and the points are displaced by DisplacementMagnitude × cos(2π t) × the displacement vectors, with t the requested time in [0, 1]. Output keeps the input structure, has no discrete time steps and adds mode_shape field arrays. Use pvWarpByVector for a single static displacement.
pitfalls: DisplacementPreapplied is true by ParaView default, so one displacement is subtracted; set it false if the input coordinates are the undeformed geometry.
Requested times are treated as a phase in [0, 1], not as physical time.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAnnotateAttributeData.explanation: Produces a one-cell text table showing Prefix followed by one value of an array: element ElementId of the chosen point, cell, field or row array, taken from MPI rank ProcessId. Use it to label an image with a probe value or a global quantity such as a residual. Input must be a non-composite dataset or a table; ParaView needs its Python support for this filter.
pitfalls: Composite datasets are not supported; extract a block first (extractBlock).
ElementId indexes the array's tuples from 0; check the index after any filter that reorders points or cells.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAnnotateGlobalData.explanation: Turns one value of a field-data (global) array into a text table: Prefix, the value formatted with Format, then Suffix, e.g. "Value is: 1.234e+05". If the array has one entry per time step it is indexed by the current time step, so the text follows the animation. The output is a one-row text table for display as an annotation, not a dataset to process further.
pitfalls: Only field (global) arrays qualify; point and cell arrays are not listed.
Format is a C printf pattern and must match the array type: %g/%f/%e for floating point, %d for integers; a mismatch makes ParaView warn and drop the value.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAnnotateSelection.explanation: Adds a string array named "Annotate Selection" to the points or cells of Input, labelling each element selected by node i of the Selection with Labels[i] and every other element with DefaultLabel. Use it to tag regions (e.g. inlet, outlet) for colouring or export. The output is the input dataset with the extra array.
pitfalls: The number of Labels must equal the number of selection nodes; otherwise ParaView warns and the output stays empty.
Only POINT or CELL selections whose nodes hold element indices are labelled; convert other selection types to INDICES with pvConvertSelection.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAnnotateTime.explanation: Source (no input) that produces a one-cell table whose Text column holds the requested animation time formatted with Format, e.g. "Time: 0.250000". It reports the time the pipeline asks it to update, not a dataset's time; when no time is requested the text is "?". Use pvAnnotateTimeFilter to label the time of a particular dataset, and pvText for fixed text.
pitfalls: Format uses fmt syntax with the argument {time}; legacy printf %f is converted with a warning.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAnnotateTimeFilter.explanation: Produces a one-row text table showing the input's current time, transformed as time × Scale + Shift and formatted with an fmt-style Format such as "Time: {time:.3f} s". Use it to label animations or images with physical time. It needs a time-dependent input; pvAnnotateTime is the source variant that needs no input.
pitfalls: Format uses fmt/Python brace syntax with the name time; old printf patterns such as "%f" are converted with a warning.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAppendArcLength.explanation: Deprecated alias of pvPolylineLength: ParaView 5.13 marks AppendArcLength for removal in 5.14. It runs the same vtkAppendArcLength filter, adding a point array arc_length with the distance along each polyline from its first point (0 for points of other cell types).
pitfalls: Use pvPolylineLength in new workflows; this identifier is expected to disappear when ParaView 5.14 is absorbed.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAppendAttributes.explanation: Combines the point and cell arrays of several inputs that share the same geometry: the output copies the first input's geometry and adds every array from all inputs. Inputs whose point or cell count differs from the first are ignored for that attribute type, and a repeated array name gets the suffix _input_<n>. Use it to gather fields computed on separate branches of one mesh (e.g. gradient and cellSize results) into one node; use append or pvAppendDatasets to join different meshes.
pitfalls: Only counts are checked, not point order or coordinates; inputs from differently numbered meshes silently attach values to the wrong points.
Duplicate array names are renamed, not replaced; check names before later nodes refer to them.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAppendDatasets.explanation: Merges the meshes of several datasets into one. With OutputDataSetType Unstructured Grid (ParaView default) inputs of almost any type are appended; with Polygonal Mesh only polydata inputs are merged and the rest are left out. Only point and cell arrays present on every input are kept, and coincident points are not merged. Use it to combine separate nodes, e.g. two clipped regions; append is the curated equivalent, pvAppendGeometry keeps polydata, and merge or pvMergeBlocks flatten one composite input.
pitfalls: Composite (multiblock) inputs are not accepted; flatten them with merge first.
Arrays missing from any one input are dropped; make names agree, e.g. with pvRenameArrays.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAppendGeometry.explanation: Appends several polygonal datasets (vtkPolyData) into one polydata, keeping vertices, lines, polygons and strips; only arrays present on every input survive and points are not merged. Use it to combine surfaces or lines from several nodes while staying polydata, e.g. for a surface writer; appendGeometry is the curated equivalent and pvAppendDatasets accepts mixed types.
pitfalls: Every input must be polydata; extract surfaces of volume meshes first.
Arrays that exist on only some inputs disappear from the result.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAppendLocationAttributes.explanation: Adds point coordinates and cell centres as data arrays: PointLocations (3-component point array, a copy of each point's coordinates) and CellCenters (3-component cell array). Geometry and existing arrays are unchanged. Use it when a calculator, export or table needs coordinates as ordinary arrays, e.g. to compute a radius or write x, y, z to CSV. This is the old name of the same ParaView filter.
pitfalls: ParaView 5.13 marks this proxy deprecated (renamed Coordinates, removal planned for 5.14); use pvCoordinates, which has the same behaviour and settings.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAppendMolecule.explanation: Appends one or more molecules (vtkMolecule) into a single molecule containing all atoms and bonds with their atom and bond data. The inputs must carry the same data arrays (same number and names). Use it to assemble a system from several molecule readers or pvConvertIntoMolecule nodes before bonding, rendering or export.
pitfalls: VTK merges atoms at identical positions by default (MergeCoincidentAtoms, not exposed in ParaView), so overlapping copies of a structure collapse into one.
Inputs with differing atom or bond arrays are not reconciled; give all inputs the same arrays.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAppendReduce.explanation: Parallel data-movement filter (vtkReductionFilter with vtkAppendFilter as the post-gather helper): it gathers the pieces of a distributed dataset from all MPI processes and appends them into one unstructured grid on one process or on every process. Use it in MPI runs when a later step needs the whole dataset in one place; in a serial run there is only process 0, so it just appends the single piece. Input must be a non-composite vtkDataSet. To combine separate nodes use append or merge.
pitfalls: Gathering a large mesh onto one process can exceed that process's memory.
Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvAppendSelections.explanation: Combines several selections (vtkSelection), for example ID, block and threshold selections, into one (vtkAppendSelection). With no Expression the inputs are joined with OR; with an Expression such as "(A|B)&!C" the inputs, named by SelectionNames in input order, are combined with | (or), & (and), ^ (xor) and ! (not). InsideOut inverts the result. A selection is not a dataset: connect it to the Selection input of pvExtractSelection, pvPlotSelectionOverTime or pvAnnotateSelection; it cannot be published as geometry.
pitfalls: When Expression is set, give exactly one name per input; otherwise the native filter fails.
Inputs should use the same FieldType (all cells or all points); the filter does not check this.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvArrow.explanation: Creates a 3-D arrow of total length 1 along +x from the origin: a cylindrical shaft joined to a conical tip, as polydata without normals. Use it as a glyph shape or annotation; scale and orient it with a transform, or use pvGlyph to place many arrows on vector data.
pitfalls: Normals are not generated, so the arrow renders faceted; apply the normals operation for smooth shading.
TipLength, ShaftRadius and TipRadius are fractions of the unit arrow length, not absolute sizes.
Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

pvAxes.explanation: Creates three line segments along the x, y and z directions from Origin, as polydata with normals and a point scalar "Axes" (0 on the x line, 0.25 on y, 0.5 on z), so colouring by that array distinguishes the axes. Each line has length ScaleFactor, or runs from -ScaleFactor to +ScaleFactor when Symmetric is true. Use it as an orientation reference in a scene.
pitfalls: The axis colours depend on the colour map applied to "Axes"; the native documentation's colour descriptions are inconsistent, so check the rendered result.
Lines are dataset geometry with no arrowheads or labels; scale them to the data with ScaleFactor.
Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

pvAxisAlignedSlice.explanation: Slices hyper tree grids and overlapping AMR data with an axis-aligned plane while keeping the input type, so a 3-D hyper tree grid becomes 2-D hyper tree grids. For hyper tree grids each entry of OffsetValues gives one slice and the output is a partitioned dataset collection; for AMR one slice at the plane is produced, at resolution Level. Use slice or pvSlice for ordinary meshes.
pitfalls: Only vtkHyperTreeGrid and vtkOverlappingAMR inputs are accepted.
The cut plane must be axis-aligned; oblique normals are not supported.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvBDFReader.explanation: Reads a Nastran Bulk Data File (.bdf) in free-field format into an unstructured grid. Only a small subset of entries is understood: GRID points, CTRIA3 triangles, PLOAD2 pressure loads (a cell array) and TITLE and TIME (field data); other entries such as CQUAD4 or CTETRA are skipped with a warning listing them. Use it for triangulated Nastran surfaces with pressure loads, not for general finite-element models.
pitfalls: Fixed-field (8-character column) BDF files are not supported; convert them to free-field (comma-separated) format.
Check the reader's warning for skipped entries; a model with only quadrilaterals or solids yields points without cells.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvBYUReader.explanation: Reads Movie.BYU geometry files (.g) into polydata made of polygons. Use it for legacy surface models in this format; companion displacement, scalar or texture files supported by vtkBYUReader are not exposed by the ParaView proxy, so only the geometry is read.
pitfalls: Coordinates are used as written; check the unit before combining with other data.

Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

pvBlockIds.explanation: Adds a cell array named BlockIdScalars to every block of a multiblock dataset, holding the index of the block (unsigned char), so blocks can be coloured, thresholded or counted by block. The input must be a vtkMultiBlockDataSet; structure and other arrays are unchanged. Use extractBlock to keep selected blocks instead.
pitfalls: Partitioned dataset collections (e.g. from newer readers) are not multiblock; the input domain rejects them.
The index is a traversal counter, not the block name; keep names via the reader's block list.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvBlockScalars.explanation: Adds a cell array named BlockIdScalars to every block of a multiblock dataset, holding the index of the block (unsigned char), so blocks can be coloured, thresholded or counted by block. The input must be a vtkMultiBlockDataSet; structure and other arrays are unchanged. This is the old name of the same ParaView filter.
pitfalls: ParaView 5.13 marks this proxy deprecated (renamed BlockIds, removal planned for 5.14); use pvBlockIds, which has the same behaviour and settings.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvBlockSelectionSource.explanation: Creates a block selection: a vtkSelection naming whole blocks of a composite dataset by their flat (composite) index, so pvExtractSelection keeps just those blocks. Choose it when you know the numeric block indices; pvBlockSelectorsSelectionSource selects blocks by path, which is more robust, and extractBlock or pvExtractBlock extract blocks directly without a selection. A selection is not a dataset: connect it to the Selection input of pvExtractSelection, pvPlotSelectionOverTime or pvAnnotateSelection; it cannot be published as geometry.
pitfalls: Flat indices count every node of the composite tree in depth-first order, including the root (0) and intermediate multiblocks, so the first leaf is usually 1 or more.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvBlockSelectorsSelectionSource.explanation: Creates a block selection from selector paths (vtkPVSelectionSource with BLOCK_SELECTORS content): XPath-style expressions such as "/Root/internalMesh" or "//patch" evaluated against a data assembly of the composite dataset, by default ParaView's Hierarchy. Choose it over pvBlockSelectionSource when block names are known but indices may change. A selection is not a dataset: connect it to the Selection input of pvExtractSelection, pvPlotSelectionOverTime or pvAnnotateSelection; it cannot be published as geometry.
pitfalls: Block names in the Hierarchy assembly are made path-safe: characters other than letters, digits, '.', '-' and '_' are dropped, so "Level 0" becomes Level0.
