Keep the .smv file in the same folder as the files it lists; their paths are resolved relative to it.

Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

pvFFTOfSelectionOverTime.explanation: ParaView's compound filter that extracts the values of selected points or cells over all time steps (as Plot Selection Over Time does) and applies a discrete Fourier transform to each resulting time series (Table FFT), producing tables for spectral plots. Connect Input to the temporal dataset and Selection to a selection-source node (e.g. pvIDSelectionSource or pvLocationSelectionSource). Use it to find dominant frequencies of probe signals such as vortex shedding; use pvPlotSelectionOverTime and pvTableFFT separately when you need the frequency column or windowing.
pitfalls: The compound definition disables the frequency column and uses a rectangular window and a two-sided spectrum, so rows are frequency bins without frequency labels.
Every time step of the input is executed; long series are slow, and uneven time spacing invalidates the FFT assumption of constant sampling.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvFLASHAMRParticlesReader.explanation: Reads particles from a FLASH HDF5 checkpoint or plot file into a multiblock dataset of polydata particle points with the selected particle arrays. Frequency keeps every N-th particle and FilterLocation keeps only particles inside a box. Use pvFlashReader for the grid fields of the same FLASH output.
pitfalls: MaxLocation is the upper corner of the filter box, although ParaView's own documentation calls it the minimum.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvFacetReader.explanation: Reads a Facet file (.facet): a simple ASCII format listing point coordinates and the polygons connecting them, producing polygonal data. Use it for legacy surface geometry exported in this format; for common CAD exchange use readSTL or readPLY.
pitfalls: Facet files carry no units; check the coordinate scale against other data.
Schemaxis generates this reader binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check with a sample file of this format.

pvFastUniformGrid.explanation: Synthetic source producing a 3-D uniform grid (image data) with cheap analytic point arrays: X (the x index, active scalars), optionally DistanceSquared (squared distance from the origin) and Swirl (the vector (y, z, x)). Use it for tests, benchmarks and demonstrations that need a predictable volume of adjustable size; use wavelet for a smoothly varying scalar field.
pitfalls: Values are computed from index coordinates (unit spacing, origin at index 0); they are not physical quantities.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvFeatureEdges.explanation: Full native Feature Edges: extracts boundary, feature, non-manifold and (optionally) manifold edges of a polygonal surface as polydata lines, with the same classes and ParaView defaults as featureEdges (boundary, feature and non-manifold on, manifold off, FeatureAngle 30°). It also exposes Coloring, which adds a cell array identifying each edge's class so the classes can be coloured or thresholded separately.
pitfalls: Input must be polydata; extract the surface of volume meshes first.
Inconsistent normals or duplicate points produce spurious feature or boundary edges; run normals and clean first.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvFidesJSONReader.explanation: Reads ADIOS2 data through Fides using an explicit Fides data model given as a JSON file, which describes how ADIOS2 variables form coordinates, cells and fields. The data model names one or more data sources, and DataSourcePath tells the reader which BP file or stream each source is. The output is a partitioned dataset collection. ParaView marks this route as mainly for debugging data models; use pvFidesReader when the BP output carries its own Fides metadata.
sources: ParaView 5.13.3 VTK/ThirdParty/fides/vtkfides/fides/DataSource.cxx:97-98 (the address string is converted to a pointer and dereferenced)
ParaView 5.13.3 Remoting/Application/Resources/proxies_fides.xml:68-81 (DataSourceIO documented as the address of an ADIOS::IO object)
pitfalls: Without a DataSourcePath for each source named in the JSON model nothing can be read; give the source name exactly as in the JSON.
ParaView's DataSourceIO is not exposed: it takes the memory address of a live ADIOS2 object, which Fides dereferences.
Schemaxis generates this reader binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check with a sample file of this format.

pvFidesReader.explanation: Reads ADIOS2 output through the Fides library, which maps ADIOS2 variables to meshes using a data model; for a BP file or BP4/BP5 directory written with Fides metadata the data model is found automatically. The output is a partitioned dataset collection with the selected point, cell and field arrays and the stored time steps. Use it for Fides-annotated simulation output; use pvFidesJSONReader when the data model is a separate JSON file.
sources: ParaView 5.13.3 VTK/ThirdParty/fides/vtkfides/fides/DataSource.cxx:97-98 (the address string is converted to a pointer and dereferenced)
ParaView 5.13.3 Remoting/Application/Resources/proxies_fides.xml:68-81 (DataSourceIO documented as the address of an ADIOS::IO object)
pitfalls: Array selections are made from names found in the file; list the arrays you need, because ParaView chooses the initial selection.

Streaming (StreamSteps, SST engines) is for in-situ coupling; leave it unset for files on disk. ParaView's DataSourceIO is not exposed because it takes the memory address of a live ADIOS2 object, which Fides dereferences and which is meaningless outside a co-resident simulation.
Schemaxis generates this reader binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check with a sample file of this format.

pvFieldArraysFromFile.explanation: Passes its input through unchanged and attaches the field-data arrays found in a legacy VTK file (.vtk, read with vtkDataObjectReader, e.g. a file holding a FIELD section); on a composite input every block receives them. Only field data (whole-dataset values such as run parameters, metadata or small history tables) is added, never point or cell arrays. Use it to carry case metadata alongside a mesh; for per-point or per-cell values join data with another operation instead.
pitfalls: The file must be a legacy .vtk data file; XML VTK files are not read by this filter.
An added array replaces an existing field array of the same name.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvFieldDatatoAttribute.explanation: Copies field-data arrays (one value per dataset, e.g. a time value or a parameter stored by a reader) into point or cell arrays holding that value at every point or cell. Only the first component of the first tuple is used, stored as a constant (implicit) array, so the memory cost is small; string arrays are not supported. Use it to colour, threshold or calculate with dataset-level values alongside the fields.
pitfalls: Multi-component or multi-value field arrays are reduced to their first value.
OutputFieldType is chosen by the ParaView entry text ("Point Data", "Cell Data", "Vertex Data", "Edge Data" or "Row Data"); ParaView offers only the associations the connected input has.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvFiniteElementFieldDistributor.explanation: Turns element-wise finite-element coefficients into point fields for visualization: it duplicates points so each element owns its own nodes, promotes cells to higher-order Lagrange types where needed, and evaluates H(Grad) discontinuous-Galerkin scalars and H(Curl)/H(Div) vector fields at those nodes. Input must be a partitioned dataset collection whose field data has an "Information Records" string array describing bases and fields (Intrepid2 conventions, e.g. Exodus files read with the IOSS reader); the output has the same structure with the distributed point arrays.
pitfalls: Without a valid Information Records array the filter fails; ordinary meshes are not suitable.
Pyramid elements are not supported, and the duplicated points make the output larger than the input.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvFlashReader.explanation: Reads output of the FLASH astrophysics code (HDF5 plot or checkpoint files) into an overlapping AMR (hierarchical box) dataset: nested refinement levels of uniform blocks with cell-centred variables. Level sets the finest level loaded, counted from the root level 0 (ParaView default 1), and every variable starts disabled, so name the ones you need in CellArrayStatus. Several files form a time series. For particles use pvFLASHAMRParticlesReader; to analyse on a uniform grid, follow with pvResampleToImage or pvResampleAMR.
pitfalls: The native help text says this reader loads 'Enzo format'; that is a copy error in the ParaView XML. It reads FLASH files; use pvEnzoReader for Enzo.
Level 1 shows only the two coarsest levels; raise it (up to the file's level count) before measuring fine-scale features, accepting more memory.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvFluentCFFCaseReader.explanation: Reads ANSYS Fluent results in the HDF5-based Common Fluids Format: the case file (.cas.h5) and, automatically, the data file of the same name (.dat.h5). The output is a multiblock dataset of unstructured grids with cell-centred solution fields. Several case files form a time series. Use pvFluentCaseReader for the legacy .cas/.dat format.

Unlike a mean filter it removes isolated outliers (salt-and-pepper or shot noise) while keeping sharp edges. Each component is filtered separately. Near the image border the neighbourhood is clipped to the image.
pitfalls: With the ParaView default kernel [1, 1, 1] nothing changes; set e.g. [3, 3, 1] for a 2-D image or [3, 3, 3] for a volume.
Even kernel sizes are off-centre and average the two middle values; prefer odd sizes.

pvMergeBlocks.explanation: Full native Merge Blocks: appends the leaf datasets of a composite input into one dataset. OutputDataSetType decides the result: Unstructured Grid (ParaView default) merges blocks of any type, Polygonal Mesh merges only polydata blocks and leaves others out. Use merge for the common case (merge everything with point merging); use this when you need polydata output, a merge tolerance or partition-only merging.

pvMergeTime.explanation: Combines several time-dependent inputs into one multiblock dataset (one block per input) whose time steps are the union of the inputs' times, or their intersection with Intersection on, with near-duplicates removed using Tolerance. For each requested time, every input supplies the matching step within tolerance, otherwise its last step before that time. Use it to view or export sources with different output times together.

pvMeshQuality.explanation: Adds a cell array Quality rating the shape of each cell with a Verdict metric chosen per cell type (triangle, quad, tetrahedron, pyramid, wedge, hexahedron); other cell types get 0. Use it to locate distorted or degenerate cells before a simulation or to explain solver problems. Each metric has its own scale and ideal value (for example Scaled Jacobian is 1 for an ideal element and negative for inverted ones), so read thresholds from the Verdict documentation. ParaView's defaults are Radius Ratio (triangles, tetrahedra), Edge Ratio (quads, wedges), Shape (pyramids) and Maximum Aspect Frobenius (hexahedra). Use pvCellSize or cellSize for cell size.

pvMinMax.explanation: Computes, for every point and cell array of the input, the componentwise minimum, maximum or sum over all tuples, and outputs a polydata with exactly one point and one vertex cell that carries the results under the original array names. Use it for one-number summaries such as peak temperature. In parallel runs ghost arrays are needed to avoid double counting. For cell-size-weighted totals use integrate; for distributions use pvHistogram.

pvMinkowskiFilter.explanation: Computes Minkowski functionals and shapefinders for each polyhedral cell of a Voronoi tessellation (vtkMinkowskiFilter). It adds cell arrays S (surface area), V (volume, copied from the input's Volumes array), C (integrated mean curvature), X (Euler characteristic), G (genus), T = 3V/S (thickness), B = S/C (breadth), L = C/(4 pi (G + 1)) (length), and planarity P and filamentarity F, which characterize whether a structure is sheet-like or filament-like. Use it on merged Voronoi regions from pvVoronoiMergeConnected.

Lengths and areas are in the dataset's coordinate units; no conversion is applied.

pvMotionFXCFGReader.explanation: Reads a MotionFX .cfg motion definition: rigid-body motions (such as translation, rotation or planetary motion) applied to STL bodies listed in the file. pvMulticorrelativeStatistics.explanation: Computes the mean vector and covariance matrix (with its Cholesky decomposition) of the selected arrays, i.e. a multivariate Gaussian model, and assesses each observation by its squared Mahalanobis distance from the mean, useful for outlier detection across several correlated fields. Use pvPrincipalComponentAnalysis to add eigen-decomposition. Task 3 (Model and assess the same data) assesses data that also trained the model, which flatters the fit; prefer a separate data set via ModelInput.

pvNek5000Reader.explanation: Reads Nek5000 spectral-element results through a .nek5000 metadata file that names the field-file template and the time steps. The output is an unstructured grid built from each spectral element's nodal points, with the selected fields as point arrays. Each element keeps its own copy of points shared with its neighbours unless MergePointstoCleangrid is enabled. This is a distributed reader.

VerticalDimension chooses single-layer, midpoint (lev) or interface (ilev) variables; ParaView's default is midpoint layers. Use pvNetCDFReader for CF-convention gridded files.

The output is polydata of arrows, typically rendered over the surface to check normal orientation, e.g. before extrusion, offsets or boundary-condition assignment. pvOMETIFFChannelCalculator.explanation: Combines up to ten fluorescence-microscopy channels of an OME-TIFF image into one RGBA colour image. Lookup tables and weights are keyed by the names Channel_1 to Channel_10; arrays with other names cannot be given a lookup table.

pvOMETIFFReader.explanation: Reads an OME-TIFF microscopy file (.ome.tif, .ome.tiff), using its OME-XML metadata to split the TIFF pages into z-planes, channels and time steps; the output is uniform image data with time steps. pvObjectFileFormatOFFReader.explanation: Reads Object File Format geometry (.off: vertex list followed by polygon faces) into polydata with polygons and lines. Use it for meshes from geometry-processing tools; for CAD surfaces in STL or OBJ use readSTL/pvSTLReader or pvWavefrontOBJReader.

pvOctreeImagetoPointSet.explanation: Reverses pvPointSetToOctreeImage: reads an image whose cell scalars are the unsigned-char "octree" bit mask and emits polydata with one point for every set bit, placed at the centre of the corresponding octant of the cell (a quarter of the spacing from the cell centre). Use the curated foam operation for the common case (decomposed case, internalMesh only, 0 kept); use this one for point or Lagrangian fields, zones, binary label/scalar sizes and the other native options.

pvOpenVDBReader.explanation: Reads an OpenVDB (.vdb) file, the sparse volume format used in visual effects and some simulation tools. pitfalls: The order in which arriving files are taken is decided by the native reader and has not been checked by Schemaxis.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.

pvRandomAttributes.explanation: Adds random-valued arrays to a dataset, composite dataset or hyper-tree grid: point and/or cell scalars (1 component) and vectors (3 components) of the chosen DataType, each component drawn between the two ComponentRange values. By ParaView default only cell vectors of unsigned char in [0, 255] are generated. Generated arrays become the active attributes. Use it for test data or to colour blocks distinctly (AttributesConstantPerBlock).
pitfalls: Values are pseudo-random and not guaranteed reproducible between runs; do not use them in results that are compared exactly.
Integer data types truncate the range; use Float or Double for continuous values.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRandomVectors.explanation: Adds a point array BrownianVectors of random 3-D vectors (random direction, length drawn between MinimumSpeed and MaximumSpeed) and makes it the active vectors; existing vectors are not copied as active. Output has the input's type. Use it for test vector fields or to jitter points with a warp.
pitfalls: The random sequence is not seeded by the filter, so values differ between runs.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRectilinearDatatoPointSet.explanation: Converts a rectilinear grid (axis-aligned with per-axis coordinate arrays) into an equivalent structured grid with explicit point coordinates; arrays are kept. Use it before operations that need explicit points or reject rectilinear grids.
pitfalls: Output memory grows by three coordinates per point.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRectilinearGridConnectivity.explanation: Extracts material fragments from rectilinear-grid data (single grids or multiblock collections, typically CTH results) using cell-centred volume-fraction arrays and an isovalue. Fragments are built at sub-cell resolution with an extended marching-cubes table, connected across blocks and MPI processes, and returned as a multiblock dataset with one polydata block per material; cell data carry FragmentId and the integrated attributes such as MaterialVolume. Choose it for fragment counting and volume integration on rectilinear CTH data; for AMR input use pvMaterialInterfaceFilter or pvAMRFragmentsFilter.
pitfalls: Select at least one volume-fraction array; none is selected by default, so the filter produces nothing until you name one.
All selected volume-fraction arrays must have the same data type; mixing float, double and unsigned-char arrays stops the filter.
Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI or client-server behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRectilinearGridGeometryFilter.explanation: Converts a rectilinear grid (vtkRectilinearGrid: axis-aligned cells with separate coordinate arrays along x, y and z) into polygonal data. VTK can restrict this to an i-j-k extent, but ParaView exposes no extent, so the whole grid is used: a 3-D grid becomes a cloud of vertices (one per grid point), a 2-D grid a surface of quadrilaterals and a 1-D grid a polyline, with point and cell data carried over. Use surface or pvExtractSurface to get the outer surface of a 3-D grid instead.
sources: https://gitlab.kitware.com/vtk/vtk/-/raw/v9.4.1/Filters/Geometry/vtkRectilinearGridGeometryFilter.cxx (whole extent by default; FillInputPortInformation requires vtkRectilinearGrid)
pitfalls: Only vtkRectilinearGrid input works: the ParaView domain accepts any dataset, but the VTK class requires a rectilinear grid, so other inputs fail natively.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRedistributeDataSet.explanation: Load-balances a dataset across MPI processes: it computes spatial cuts for the requested number of partitions and moves cells accordingly, assigning boundary cells to one region (ParaView default), duplicating them (marked as duplicate ghost cells) or splitting them. Output is an unstructured grid per process, or a vtkPartitionedDataSet with PreservePartitionsInOutput, and global cell ids can be generated. With default settings a serial run has one partition, so the main effect is conversion to an unstructured grid. It is the newer alternative to pvD3.
pitfalls: Image, rectilinear and structured grids become explicit unstructured grids, which can need much more memory; ParaView warns about this.
Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvReductionFilter.explanation: Generic parallel reduction (vtkReductionFilter): an optional pre-gather algorithm runs on each MPI process, the results are gathered, and a post-gather algorithm combines them on one or all processes. The helpers are named by VTK class name (PreGatherHelperName, PostGatherHelperName); the helper proxies themselves cannot be set in Schemaxis. In a serial run there is a single piece, so the operation mainly applies the helpers to it. Prefer pvAppendReduce for the common gather-and-append case.
pitfalls: This proxy's ReductionMode labels for values 0 and 1 are swapped relative to VTK's meaning; read the ReductionMode help before choosing.
Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvReflect.explanation: Mirrors the input across an axis-aligned plane and outputs an unstructured grid containing, by ParaView default, both the original and the mirrored copy (CopyInput). The plane is either a face of the input bounding box (X Min to Z Max) or x, y or z = Center. Vectors, normals and tensors are flipped; with FlipAllInputArrays (default true) every signed 3-, 6- or 9-component array is treated as a vector or tensor too. Use it to complete a symmetric half-model; the curated reflect uses the same filter with Schemaxis defaults (plane X at 0).
pitfalls: ParaView's default plane is X Min, the minimum-x face of the bounding box, not x = 0; choose X with Center 0 for a symmetry plane at the origin.
The two halves are not merged, so points on the mirror plane are duplicated; run cleanGrid if connectivity across the plane matters.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRemoteSourceProxy.explanation: ParaView's Remote Source Proxy (vtkPVMultiServerDataSource) mirrors, inside the client's built-in session, a dataset that lives on another server in a multi-server ParaView setup. It has no inputs or file and receives its data only through a native DependencyLink to that external proxy, which Schemaxis does not expose (it is listed as a property gap). In a Schemaxis workflow it therefore has nothing to fetch and is not a useful data source; use a reader or a source operation instead.
pitfalls: The DependencyLink binding is an unsupported native property class, so the node cannot be connected to remote data from authored input.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRemoveGhostInformation.explanation: Removes ghost cells and the vtkGhostType point and cell arrays from polydata or unstructured grids; for hyper tree grids it removes the ghost array and masks the ghost cells. Use it before writing or measuring data from a parallel pipeline so duplicated boundary layers are not exported or counted twice.
pitfalls: Only polydata, unstructured grid and hyper tree grid inputs are accepted; for structured data use pvExtractSubset to trim ghost layers.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRenameArrays.explanation: Passes its input through unchanged except for array names. Each list property holds [current name, new name] pairs for one attribute type: points, cells, field data, graph vertices, graph edges or table rows. It accepts any data object, including composites and tables. Use it to give arrays the names a later step expects, e.g. to make datasets agree before pvAppendDatasets, or to replace solver names before export.
pitfalls: Each list is flat: current name, then new name, repeated. Schemaxis rejects a list with an odd number of entries (INVALID_LENGTH) before the node runs.
New names must stay unique within an attribute type; renaming onto an existing name creates a clash.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvResampleAMR.explanation: Samples overlapping AMR data (vtkOverlappingAMR) onto a uniform grid covering the box from Min to Max with NumberofSamples points per axis, taking each value from the finest level that covers the sample. The result is a multiblock of uniform-grid partitions (NumberOfPartitions) with the fields on points (TransferToNodes true) or cells. Use it to compare AMR results with regular-grid data or to export a fixed-resolution image; use pvConvertAMRdatasettoMultiblock to keep the native blocks.
pitfalls: Min and Max both start at [0, 0, 0], which describes no region; always set the box.
Parts of the box outside the AMR domain are trimmed, so the grid may have fewer points than requested.
Input data are assumed cell-centred and rectilinear AMR is not supported.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvResampleToImage.explanation: Samples the input's point and cell arrays onto a new uniform image (vtkImageData) with SamplingDimensions points along x, y and z, spanning the input bounds (UseInputBounds, ParaView default) or custom SamplingBounds. Values are interpolated at the image points by a probe filter, so cell arrays also become point arrays, and points outside the input get 0 in the vtkValidPointMask array. Use it to convert unstructured results to a regular grid for image writers, volume rendering or pvHistogram2D; resample probes onto an existing mesh instead.
pitfalls: Memory grows with the product of the dimensions: the default 100 × 100 × 100 is a million points per array.
Sampling is point-wise without averaging, so features smaller than the spacing can be missed.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvResampleToLine.explanation: Same native filter as pvPlotOverLine (vtkPVProbeLineFilter) with a different starting configuration: uniform sampling with Resolution 40 and the SamplingPattern hidden in ParaView's GUI. It returns a polyline with the input arrays interpolated along Point1-Point2 plus arc_length and vtkValidPointMask. Use it for a light uniform resampling, e.g. a coarse profile to compare between runs; use pvPlotOverLine or probeLine for detailed profiles.
pitfalls: Omitted, Point1 and Point2 are never the static [0, 0, 0]: in a bounded native probe with a polydata upstream a batch run read (1, 1, 1) and (-1, -1, -1), a line unrelated to the data (composite inputs give other uninitialised-bounds corners, by the source), and when the upstream already had data they were the corners of its bounding box. Always set both.
Points outside the data are flagged by vtkValidPointMask 0; exclude them before computing statistics.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvResampleWithDataset.explanation: Samples the arrays of SourceDataArrays at the points of DestinationMesh: the output has the destination's geometry and structure, and its point data holds the source's point and cell values interpolated at each destination point plus a vtkValidPointMask array marking points found inside the source. Both inputs may be composite. Use it to transfer a solution onto another mesh, e.g. CFD results onto a structural or measurement mesh; resample is the curated version and pvResampleToImage samples onto a generated image.
pitfalls: Sampled values are always point data, even for cell-centred source fields.
Destination points outside the source have vtkValidPointMask 0 and meaningless values; filter on the mask or enable MarkBlankPointsAndCells.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvResourceImageTexture.explanation: Typed texture resource (vtkTexture) that loads its image from a file such as a PNG or JPEG. It produces no dataset: other nodes reference it through texture inputs, currently pvLogo's Texture port, and several consumers may share it. Use it when the picture is a file on disk; use pvResourceTexture when the image comes from a pipeline node.
pitfalls: FileName is required and is read by ParaView's image reader; unsupported image formats fail at update.
Exercised by examples/schemaxis/paraview-textures.json (receipt in verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json); other settings are unverified.

pvResourcePVLookupTable.explanation: Typed colour lookup-table resource (vtkPVDiscretizableColorTransferFunction) that maps data values to colours, either as a continuous colour map defined by RGBPoints control points or as categorical colours for annotated values (InterpretValuesAsCategories). It is not a dataset: it is connected to lookup-table inputs such as pvColorByArray, pvOMETIFFChannelCalculator or the PLY and OpenVDB writers, and several consumers can share one table. Scene appearances build their own colour maps from field, range and preset, so use this resource only for those explicit ports.
pitfalls: RGBPoints positions are data values; ParaView's GUI usually rescales a new map to the data range, but here nothing rescales it, so set positions that cover your array's range.
Optional ScalarOpacityFunction and TransferFunction2D inputs accept pvResourcePiecewiseFunction and pvResourceTransferFunction2D nodes.
Exercised by examples/schemaxis/paraview-resources.json and paraview-writer-resources.json (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json); other settings are unverified.

pvResourcePiecewiseFunction.explanation: Typed piecewise-function resource (vtkPiecewiseFunction) that maps a data value to a single number, normally opacity from 0 to 1, through control points. Its main use is the ScalarOpacityFunction input of pvResourcePVLookupTable, where it defines how transparent each data value is. It produces no dataset and can be shared by several lookup tables.
pitfalls: Points positions are data values and are not rescaled automatically; place them across your array's range.
Exercised by examples/schemaxis/paraview-resources.json (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json); other settings are unverified.

pvResourceTexture.explanation: Typed texture resource (vtkTexture) whose image comes from a connected pipeline node producing image data (vtkImageData), for example a PNG series reader or a resampled field. Like pvResourceImageTexture it is referenced by texture inputs such as pvLogo's Texture port and produces no dataset of its own. Choose it when the texture must follow pipeline changes; use pvResourceImageTexture to load a file directly.
pitfalls: Input must be image data; meshes or tables are rejected by the native input domain.

Exercised by examples/schemaxis/paraview-textures.json, where file- and pipeline-backed textures gave identical data (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json resourceChecks); other inputs are unverified.

pvResourceTransferFunction2D.explanation: Typed two-dimensional transfer-function resource (vtkPVTransferFunction2D): colour and opacity defined over two axes, usually a scalar on x and a second quantity such as gradient magnitude on y, as used by ParaView's 2-D volume rendering. It is built from coloured rectangles (Boxes) within Range and sampled to an image of OutputDimensions. In Schemaxis it only connects to the TransferFunction2D input of pvResourcePVLookupTable; Schemaxis scene appearances do not perform volume rendering.
pitfalls: Creating it has no visible effect in Schemaxis images; it is relevant only if a consumer uses the lookup table's 2-D function.
Exercised by examples/schemaxis/paraview-resources.json (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json); its rendering effect is unverified.

pvRestartedSimExodusReader.explanation: Reads an Exodus simulation that was restarted, through a metadata file listing the output file sets of each restart, so they behave as one continuous time series. The output and the block, set, map and variable selections are those of pvExodusIIReader: a multiblock of unstructured grids with nodal and element variables, displacements applied by default. Use pvExodusIIReader for a single run's files.
pitfalls: FileName must name the restart metadata file, not one of the Exodus files.

FilePattern, FilePrefix and XMLFileName are optional, as their ParaView file lists are marked optional. Leave them out to read FileName as given: FilePattern and FilePrefix rebuild the file name from a printf-style pattern, so supplying them changes which file is read, and XMLFileName names an optional part and material description.
VTK's Exodus reader starts with every result variable disabled; list the PointVariables and ElementVariables you need, or the blocks arrive without fields.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRestartedSimSpyPlotReader.explanation: Reads a CTH (Spy Plot) simulation that was restarted, through a metadata file (.spcth-timeseries) listing the output file sets of each restart, so the sets behave as one continuous time series. Output port 0 is the volume data (hierarchical blocks with cell-centred arrays such as material volume fractions), port 1 the tracers and port 2 the markers; select a port with {"node": id, "port": n}. Use pvSpyPlotReader for a single .spcth case and pvspcthhistoryreader for history files.
pitfalls: FileName must name the restart metadata file, not one of the individual .spcth case files.
Fields are cell-centred; convert with cellToPoint before operations that need point data.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvReverseSense.explanation: Flips the orientation of polygonal data: ReverseCells (ParaView default true) reverses each cell's point order, which flips its implied front face, and ReverseNormals (default false) multiplies existing point and cell normals by −1. Use it when a surface's normals point inward, e.g. an STL with clockwise winding, before shading, normal-based glyphs or operations that assume outward orientation; normals with consistency orients a surface automatically.
pitfalls: Reversing cells while an existing Normals array is left unchanged makes them disagree; enable ReverseNormals too when normals are present.
ReverseNormals has no effect if the input carries no normals.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRibbon.explanation: Turns lines and polylines (polydata, e.g. streamlines) into flat ribbon strips that follow each line. The ribbon's orientation comes from a normal: the 3-component point array chosen in Vectors, or the fixed DefaultNormal when UseDefaultNormal is true; with neither, VTK computes sliding normals for each line. Width is the half-width; VaryWidth scales it along the line by the Scalars array from Width at the array minimum to twice Width at its maximum, and Angle rotates the ribbon about the line. Use tube or pvTube for round tubes.
pitfalls: The Vectors array sets the ribbon normal, not the flow direction; selecting the velocity itself, which is tangent to a streamline, gives degenerate ribbons.
Lines with duplicate consecutive points, or normals parallel to the line, are skipped; run clean first.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRotationalExtrusion.explanation: Sweeps polygonal data around an axis through the coordinate origin (RotationAxis, ParaView default z) to build a swept surface: free edges and lines become surfaces and vertices become lines, so a profile curve becomes an axisymmetric shell (cylinder, bottle), and Translation or DeltaRadius turn it into a spring or spiral. Capping closes the ends with copies of a filled 2-D input. Output is polydata, a surface rather than a volume; use pvVolumeOfRevolution to sweep 2-D cells into volume cells.
pitfalls: The axis passes through (0, 0, 0); translate the profile first (transform) if the physical axis is elsewhere.
Closed surfaces such as a sphere have no free edges, so they give no swept surface, only caps.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvRuler.explanation: ParaView's ruler: a straight line (vtkLineSource) from Point1 to Point2 that ParaView's ruler representation labels with its length. In Schemaxis the output is only the line geometry; the distance is not stored in the data, so compute it from the two points when you need the value. Use it as a distance annotation; pvLine gives a subdivided line for probing.
pitfalls: No distance array or measurement is produced by the source itself.
Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

pvSAVGReader.explanation: Reads a NIST SAVG file (.savg), a plain-text format of coloured points, lines and polygons used for immersive-visualization scenes. The output is a partitioned dataset collection with one polydata partition per primitive kind found (points, lines, polygons), with optional "rgba_colors" and "vertex_normals" point arrays. Use it to bring such scene geometry into a pipeline; it carries no simulation fields.
pitfalls: The file name must end in .savg; the reader ignores any other name and produces nothing.
Primitives such as tri, pixel, text and program lines are skipped as unsupported.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvSEPReader.explanation: Reads Stanford Exploration Project seismic data: a text .H header describing up to 32 named axes (labels such as CDP, LINE, OFFSET, DEPTH) with their sizes, origins and sampling, which points to the raw .H@ data file. You choose which named axes become the output x, y and z (or x and y for 2-D output) and hold the remaining axes at one index each; the result is uniform image data with an ImageScalars array.
pitfalls: Axis names must match the header labels; when the header has no labels, VTK assigns the default names to the first axes in order.
Choose different axes for x, y, z and the fixed dimensions; reusing one axis collapses that direction.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvSLACDataReader.explanation: Reads the NetCDF-based mesh and mode files of SLAC's accelerator electromagnetics codes (Omega3P, Tau3P and related tools). MeshFileName is the element mesh; ModeFileName is one mode file (usually an eigenmode with electric and magnetic fields) or several files forming a time series. Output port 0 (External Surface) is the boundary surface and port 1 (Entire Volume) the volume mesh, filled only when ReadInternalVolume is enabled. When a mode file stores a frequency (100 or more, treated as hertz) the complex fields are animated over one period of the lowest frequency: each mode contributes magnitude × FrequencyScale × cos(initial phase + 2πft + PhaseShift) and the modes are summed.
pitfalls: Port 0 is only the external surface; enable ReadInternalVolume and connect {"node": id, "port": 1} for fields inside the cavity.

ModeFileName is optional: omit it to read the mesh alone. A bounded native probe on 2026-10-12 (ParaView 5.13.3, serial, synthetic one-tetrahedron mesh) read the mesh with ModeFileName omitted, with no error (4 points, 4 cells); it has not been run on real SLAC files.
Mode files must use the same points as the mesh file.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.

pvSLACParticleDataReader.explanation: Reads particle data written by SLAC's accelerator codes (NetCDF files with the SLAC particle conventions) into polydata: a set of particle points in 3-D space. Several files form a time series, one file per step in the order listed. Use it with pvSLACDataReader to show particles inside the cavity fields.
pitfalls: The native reader loads everything in piece 0; it does not distribute particles across MPI processes.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.

pvSPHDatasetInterpolator.explanation: Interpolates particle data with smoothed-particle-hydrodynamics kernels: the Input is the particle set (a point set with point arrays, normally including density and optionally mass) and the Source is any dataset whose points receive the SPH-weighted values. The output keeps Source's structure and adds the interpolated arrays, a Shepard-sum array (on by default) and any derivative arrays. Use it to post-process SPH simulation output on meshes, slices or images; for non-SPH scattered data use pvPointDatasetInterpolator.
pitfalls: The kernel SpatialStep (smoothing length h) defaults to 0.0001; set it to the simulation's smoothing length in dataset units, or neighbourhoods are tiny and most output points become null points.
DensityArray defaults to the name Rho; name your particle density array if it differs.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvSPHLineInterpolator.explanation: Interpolates SPH particle data (Input) with SPH kernels onto a high-resolution straight line set in the Source options (Point1, Point2, Resolution; ParaView default 1000 intervals), producing a polyline profile with the interpolated arrays and a Shepard-sum array, e.g. a density or pressure profile through a particle simulation.
pitfalls: The line endpoints may be derived by ParaView from the input bounds, but Schemaxis has not verified that; their static default is [0, 0, 0] for both, a degenerate line. Set Point1 and Point2 explicitly in dataset coordinates.
The kernel SpatialStep (smoothing length h) defaults to 0.0001; set it to the simulation's smoothing length in dataset units, or neighbourhoods are tiny and most output points become null points.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvSPHPlaneInterpolator.explanation: Interpolates SPH particle data (Input) with SPH kernels onto a bounded plane set in the Source options (Center, Normal, BoundingBox, Padding, Resolution or CellSize), producing a planar grid of SPH-weighted values for heat-map sections through a particle simulation.
pitfalls: The plane's bounding box may be derived by ParaView from the input bounds, but Schemaxis has not verified that (static default [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1]); set BoundingBox, Center and Normal explicitly.
The kernel SpatialStep (smoothing length h) defaults to 0.0001; set it to the simulation's smoothing length in dataset units, or neighbourhoods are tiny and most output points become null points.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvSPHVolumeInterpolator.explanation: Interpolates SPH particle data (Input) with SPH kernels onto a bounded volume set in the Source options (Origin, Scale, Padding, Resolution or CellSize), producing image data that can be contoured, sliced or volume-rendered as a continuous field.
pitfalls: The volume's origin and extent may be derived by ParaView from the input bounds, but Schemaxis has not verified that (static defaults origin [0, 0, 0], scale [1, 1, 1]); set Origin, Scale and Resolution explicitly.
The kernel SpatialStep (smoothing length h) defaults to 0.0001; set it to the simulation's smoothing length in dataset units, or neighbourhoods are tiny and most output points become null points.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvSTEPReader.explanation: Reads a STEP CAD file through OpenCASCADE and tessellates its B-rep faces into triangles, giving a multiblock dataset with one polydata block per shape (named from the file, or Unnamed) and a per-cell Colors array from the CAD colours. LinearDeflection and AngularDeflection set how closely the triangles follow curved surfaces; ReadWire adds edges as polylines. Use it to bring CAD geometry in for rendering, clipping or probing; use pvIGESReader for .iges, and readSTL or pvSTLReader for already-tessellated STL.
pitfalls: VTK applies no unit conversion; compare the output bounds with the simulation's length unit before combining them.
LinearDeflection is an absolute distance in model units unless RelativeDeflection is on; the default 0.1 can be very coarse for small parts, so scale it to the model size.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.

pvSTLReader.explanation: Full native STL reader: reads ASCII or binary stereolithography files (.stl) into triangle polydata, and a list of several files into a time series. In ParaView 5.13.3 this proxy exposes only the file list (the ScalarTags option of the core reader is not exposed). For a single CAD surface the curated readSTL does the same with one file.
pitfalls: STL carries no units; check millimetres versus metres before combining with simulation data.

Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

pvScatterPlot.explanation: ParaView's Scatter Plot: passes a dataset through unchanged (vtkPassThrough) and marks it for the plot-matrix view, which shows every pair of arrays as a scatter plot in the ParaView GUI. In Schemaxis the data result is the unchanged input.
pitfalls: No plot or table is computed; to get values for plotting, convert to a table, e.g. with pvExtractAttributes.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvSegYReader.explanation: Reads a SEG-Y seismic file. 3-D surveys become a structured grid (default) or, with StructuredGrid false, a lighter image data whose positions and shape may be approximate; 2-D lines become a structured grid sheet. Axes are crossline, inline and depth, and the trace samples are the point values. Trace positions come from source, CDP or custom header bytes, and VerticalCRS decides whether the vertical axis is height (positive up) or depth.
pitfalls: The extended textual header is not read, so check VerticalCRS against the survey documentation.
In Custom XYCoordMode set both XCoordByte and YCoordByte: ParaView's initial YCoordByte is 76, not the SEG-Y source-Y byte 77.
Schemaxis generates this reader binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check with a sample file of this format.

pvSelectionQuerySource.explanation: Creates a query selection, ParaView's "Find Data" mechanism: QueryString is a structured query over the input's arrays, element indices or locations, evaluated per element when pvExtractSelection (or another extractor) runs; the elements where it is true are selected. ElementType chooses cells (ParaView default) or points, and Selectors can restrict the query to some blocks of a composite input. The output is a vtkSelection (no geometry) for the Selection port of pvExtractSelection or pvAnnotateSelection. For a plain range on one array, pvThresholdSelectionSource is simpler.
pitfalls: ParaView evaluates query text as Python (vtkPythonSelector, paraview.detail.calculator), so Schemaxis accepts only the structured QueryString, generates the text itself and checks it again before assignment; the selection still needs a ParaView build with Python and numpy.
Leave ContentType at 9 (QUERY) and FieldTypeOption at 1; the other values make this source produce a different, empty selection type.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvShrink.explanation: Moves the points of every cell toward that cell's centroid (average of its points) by ShrinkFactor, separating cells so individual elements become visible; output is an unstructured grid with unshared points. It is a mesh-inspection aid, not a geometric operation for measurements; the curated shrink offers the same with a Schemaxis default.
pitfalls: Shrunk cells no longer share points, so connectivity-based operations see disjoint cells.

pvSlice.explanation: ParaView's general Slice filter: cuts any dataset (or hyper tree grid) with an implicit surface (Plane, Box, Sphere or Cylinder) and returns polygonal data, i.e. surfaces from volumes and lines from surfaces, with point data interpolated. Otherwise s is the projection of (point − Origin) on Point1 − Origin, divided by that edge's squared length, and t likewise with Point2, so s and t are 0 at Origin and 1 at Point1 or Point2. One file supplies every time step the format stores.

ParaView 5.13.3 has no native Mili reader; the Mili plugin is an optional part of the VisIt bridge. One file supplies every time step the format stores.

pvVolumeOfRevolution.explanation: Sweeps a 2-D (planar) dataset about an axis to create a 3-D unstructured grid: vertices become lines, lines become quadrilaterals and 2-D cells become volume cells, with point and cell data copied to each swept copy. Use it to build a 3-D volume from an axisymmetric simulation for visualization or export. The axis is given by AxisPosition and AxisDirection (ParaView default: the x axis through the origin) and the sweep by SweepAngle and Resolution. ParaView's own short description of this filter (elevation) is a copying error.
pitfalls: The axis must not cross the geometry, or the output has intersecting cells.
Vector arrays such as velocity are copied unchanged to every swept copy, not rotated; their components are only meaningful in the original plane.

pvVoronoiMergeConnected.explanation: Merges the cells of a Voronoi tessellation that share the same global RegionId into single polyhedron cells (vtkPMergeConnected), turning per-particle Voronoi cells into one cell per connected region. Input is a multiblock of unstructured grids carrying RegionId on points and cells and a Volumes cell array, as produced by ParaView's cosmology Voronoi tools; output is a multiblock with merged polyhedra, RegionId and summed Volumes. pvMinkowskiFilter can then characterize the shapes.

pvVortexCores.explanation: Extracts vortex core lines with the parallel-vectors method: lines where velocity is parallel to acceleration (or to jerk with UseHigherOrderMethod). Candidate cells are prefiltered with the Q and delta criteria, and the output polylines carry q-criterion, delta-criterion, lambda_2-criterion, lambda_ci-criterion and vorticity_magnitude point arrays for further filtering. Only 3-D linear cells are processed and the vector field must be a 3-component point array. Use it to locate swirling-flow axes; for vortex regions rather than lines, compute Q or lambda2 with gradient and contour them.
pitfalls: Surface or 2-D meshes and higher-order cells produce no output; supply a linear volume mesh.
The method is sensitive to noise and finds short spurious segments; threshold the output on the criterion arrays.

pvWarpByScalar.explanation: Displaces each point along a direction by ScaleFactor × its scalar value: x' = x + ScaleFactor · s · n, with n the point normal when the input has normals and UseNormal is false, otherwise the constant Normal. XYPlane uses each point's z coordinate as s and warps along z (carpet plots). Polydata, structured and unstructured grids keep their type; image and rectilinear inputs become structured grids. Use it for elevation or carpet plots of a scalar on a surface; the curated warpScalar covers the common case.
pitfalls: If the surface has point normals they are used unless UseNormal is true, so Normal may appear to be ignored.
ScaleFactor stays 1.0 unless set (ParaView's NoDefault hint), so a scalar in pascals moves points by thousands of length units; choose a factor relative to the data range.

pvWarpByVector.explanation: Displaces each point by ScaleFactor × a 3-component point vector (x' = x + ScaleFactor · v), e.g. structural displacements or mode shapes, to show the deformed shape. Point and cell data pass through, but input normals are dropped because the geometry changed. The curated warpVector covers the common case.

pvWavelet.explanation: Generates image data over WholeExtent (spacing SubsampleRate, origin 0) with the point scalar "RTData" = Maximum·exp(-r²/(2·StandardDeviation²)) + XMag·sin(XFreq·x) + YMag·sin(YFreq·y) + ZMag·cos(ZFreq·z), where x, y, z are offsets from Center divided by the extent width on each axis and r is their length. It is ParaView's standard synthetic volume, used to test contouring, slicing, volume rendering and exports. The curated wavelet operation offers Schemaxis defaults.

It accepts structured grids, polygonal data, unstructured grids, or a multiblock containing these, and stores mesh and point/cell solution fields in one file, using HDF5 storage by default (UseHDF5) or the older ADF layout. Publication uses the semantic contract: ParaView re-reads the file and geometry plus every input point and cell field are compared, accepting changes in block structure, point identity, connectivity order and storage type. Use it to hand results to CGNS-based tools; use pvWriteXMLUnstructuredGridWriter or pvWriteXMLMultiBlockDataWriter when the data only needs to round-trip through VTK.

Use it to hand values to spreadsheets, pandas or R; mesh topology is not kept. Publication uses the table contract: Schemaxis re-reads the file and checks the row count and every input array of the written association within the export tolerance, accepting the loss of topology, coordinates and structure.

pitfalls: Precision defaults to 5 significant digits; raise it (17 reproduces doubles exactly) or set an export tolerance, otherwise verification usually fails.

Verification covers one dataset or table: composite input is rejected with UNSUPPORTED_DATA_TYPE (merge it with pvMergeBlocks first). The verifier uses the FieldAssociation, FieldDelimiter, StringDelimiter and UseStringDelimiter that ParaView holds on the created writer, so a .tsv file is checked with the tab ParaView sets for it. Author FieldAssociation as ParaView's entry text, for example "Cell Data". When it is omitted, ParaView picks (and Schemaxis reads back) the first of Point, Cell, Vertex, Edge, Row then Field Data that has arrays and tuples, which is not always the points. Only "Point Data", "Cell Data" and (for tables) "Row Data" can be verified: "Field Data", "Vertex Data" or "Edge Data" is rejected at planning with UNSUPPORTED_ASSOCIATION, and "Row Data" for a non-table input fails verification with the same fault; a delimiter longer than one character gives UNSUPPORTED_DELIMITER.
ChooseArraysToWrite true is rejected at planning (ARRAY_SELECTION_UNVERIFIABLE) because the table comparison needs every input array in the file; filter arrays with pvPassArrays and export that node.

pvWriteDataSetWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer for the legacy VTK format (.vtk), the original single-file VTK layout still read by ParaView, VisIt, many solver converters and simple scripts. Publication uses the exact contract: ParaView re-reads the file and structure, connectivity, values and storage types must match the input exactly. Prefer scene geometry or the VTK XML writers (pvWriteXMLUnstructuredGridWriter, pvWriteXMLPolyDataWriter, ...) for new work, and use this writer when a downstream tool reads only legacy .vtk files.

pvWriteEnSightWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer for EnSight Gold, the case format read by Ansys EnSight and many CFD post-processors: a .case index, a binary .geo geometry file and one file per point or cell array. It accepts only a single, non-composite unstructured grid; cells are grouped into EnSight parts by an integer BlockId cell array when present, otherwise everything is part 1. Publication uses the semantic contract: the case is read back and geometry plus every input point and cell field are compared, accepting changes in structure, point identity, connectivity order and storage type. Use pvWriteXMLUnstructuredGridWriter for lossless VTK storage, or pvWriteCGNSWriter / pvWriteIOSSWriter for other solver formats.
pitfalls: VTK names the case file data.0.case (0 is the process number); Schemaxis finds it automatically, but keep the .case, .geo and variable files together when moving them.

Only arrays with 1, 3, 6 or 9 components (scalar, vector, symmetric or full tensor) get a valid case-file entry, and pixel or voxel cells are skipped; remove such arrays with pvPassArrays and avoid grids built directly from image data, or verification fails.
Field-data arrays are not stored in EnSight, while semantic verification checks them; remove field data upstream if the input carries any.

pvWriteGenericIOWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer that saves a multiblock of particle unstructured grids as one HACC GenericIO file (.gio), each block becoming one rank's data (vtkPGenericIOMultiBlockWriter). Point coordinates are written as double variables x, y, z, single-component point arrays keep their names and 3-component arrays become <name>_x, _y and _z; cells and connectivity are not stored. Schemaxis verifies it with the semantic comparison, accepting structure and storage changes.
pitfalls: The default readback cannot set coordinate names; give readback {"operation": "pvGenericIOMultiBlockReader", "options": {"xAxis": "x", "yAxis": "y", "zAxis": "z", "PointArrayStatus": [...]}} as Schemaxis's qualification fixture does.
If the data already have point arrays named x, y or z, the coordinates are written as xx, yy or zz instead.

pvWriteHoudiniWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer for the ASCII Houdini geometry format (.geo, pre-version-12 PGEOMETRY V2), for taking surfaces into SideFX Houdini for effects or rendering. The input must be polygonal data; point arrays become point attributes, cell arrays primitive attributes, and triangle strips are split into triangles. Schemaxis verifies geometry only, with its own parser of the writer's exact grammar (vertices, lines, polygons, triangle strips, attribute brackets, and NPrims counting emitted triangles): points and primitives are compared with the triangulated input surface, accepting loss of fields, point identity, interior cells and structure. Use pvWritePOBJWriter or pvWritePSTLWriter for more widely read surface formats.
pitfalls: Coordinates are written with 6 significant digits (vtkHoudiniPolyDataWriter.cxx:383-386), so a zero tolerance is rejected at planning (INVALID_TOLERANCE) and publication rejects a tolerance below half a unit in the sixth digit of the largest coordinate (TOLERANCE_BELOW_WRITER_PRECISION, which reports the minimum). A tolerance of 1e-6 suits coordinates below 1; scale it with the data.

Verification requires the geometry comparison. The Schemaxis parser reads exactly what the writer emits: vertices, lines, polygons and triangle strips (each strip triangle counts as one NPrims primitive) with attribute values in brackets ignored. A degenerate strip of fewer than 3 points corrupts the writer's own file and gives UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT; remove such cells upstream. Array selection is not needed to verify cell arrays.
A custom readback reader is rejected for this writer; the built-in parser is always used.

pvWriteHyperTreeGridWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer for VTK's hyper tree grid XML format (.htg), which stores adaptive tree-based meshes (vtkHyperTreeGrid: a coarse grid of quadtrees or octrees) with their refinement trees, masks, coordinates and cell fields. The input must be one non-composite hyper tree grid; all its arrays are written. Publication uses the exact contract: ParaView re-reads the file and tree structure, masks, coordinates and cell arrays must match exactly. Use pvWriteSerialHTGMultiBlock for a multiblock of hyper tree grids; this is also the format scene geometry chooses for hyper tree grids.
pitfalls: Few tools outside VTK and ParaView read .htg; convert the data to an unstructured grid upstream when the receiver needs a conventional mesh.
Ascii DataMode is mainly for inspection and gives much larger files than Appended.

pvWriteIOSSWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer for Exodus II (.exo) through the IOSS library, the finite-element format of Sandia's SIERRA codes, Cubit and many structural and multiphysics solvers. It accepts a dataset, a partitioned dataset or a partitioned dataset collection; every partition becomes an element block unless selectors (or, for data read by ParaView's IOSS reader, its IOSS assembly) assign partitions to blocks and sets, and a time-dependent input is exported for the one scheduled time step: Schemaxis manages TimeStepRange and TimeStepStride, because the writer otherwise loops over every input time step itself. Publication uses the semantic contract: the file is re-read and geometry plus every input point and cell field are compared, accepting loss of structure, point identity, connectivity order and storage type. Use pvWriteExodusIIWriter for ParaView's older Exodus writer and pvWriteCGNSWriter for CGNS tools.
pitfalls: Exodus ids start at 1. For time-dependent input, ParaView 5.13.3's IOSS writer aborts the whole run when the point global ids start at 0 or are absent (native pvbatch probe, 2026-10-12), so Schemaxis refuses such an export before writing (UNSUPPORTED_INPUT): add ids with pvGlobalPointAndCellIds and set OffsetGlobalIds true, which the probe confirmed writes the scheduled step. Static input is written either way.

vtkIOSSWriter runs its own time loop and ignores the scheduled time (vtkIOSSWriter.cxx:285-342). A native pvbatch 5.13.3 probe found that on creation ParaView replaces the static TimeStepRange [0, 1] with the domain range [0, n-1], and a default export wrote all steps for one scheduled time. When the exported node reports two or more time steps (read from its pipeline information, so filters count too), Schemaxis sets TimeStepRange [k, k+1] and TimeStepStride 2 for the scheduled step k (probe: exactly one step, whose Point Value matched step k, for k = 0, 2 and 9); both settings are managed and cannot be authored, and a scheduled time that is not one of the input steps gives TIME_NOT_IN_INPUT. The probe did not establish the time stamp stored in the file, so do not rely on it.
ParaView's GUI-only entity-type chooser (EntityType, which has no native command) is not exposed; select blocks and arrays with the *Selectors and *Arrays settings.

Semantic readback compares every input point and cell array by name. Exodus stores global ids as maps rather than fields, and readers may merge arrays whose names end in X, Y and Z into one vector, so inputs carrying such arrays (for example GlobalPointIds, or Point X/Y/Z) fail verification with 'semantic readback lacks an input field'; pass only the arrays you need with pvPassArrays before exporting.

pvWriteJPEGWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer that saves image data (vtkImageData) as a JPEG (.jpg) file: 1 to 3 components of unsigned char values, compressed lossily at VTK's quality 95. Publication uses the pixels contract, comparing dimensions, components and values after re-reading, so a positive export tolerance is required (zero is rejected at planning) and pvWritePNGWriter is the choice for exact pixels.
sources: ParaView 5.13.3 VTK/IO/Image/vtkJPEGWriter.cxx:213-223 (unsigned char only, warning and no file otherwise)
pitfalls: A tolerance of 0 is rejected at planning (INVALID_TOLERANCE) because JPEG compression changes values; choose a tolerance in the 0 to 255 value range or export PNG. Verification also requires the pixels comparison.

VTK's writer accepts only unsigned char (8-bit) scalars (vtkJPEGWriter.cxx:219-223); other scalar types, or an image without active scalars, fail before writing with UNSUPPORTED_DATA_TYPE. Convert upstream, because Schemaxis performs no implicit conversion.
Schemaxis manages the file name, so export 2-D images; a numbered 3-D stack needs a file pattern.

pvWriteJSONImageWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer that saves a uniform image (vtkImageData) node as a JSON document listing the image dimensions, origin, spacing and the values of its point arrays, for web or scripting tools rather than for re-reading in ParaView. Use it as an export `writer` with comparison "pixels": Schemaxis then parses the JSON itself and checks dimensions, origin, spacing and exactly the arrays the writer emits against the source image: one-component point arrays other than vtkValidPointMask, narrowed by ArrayName and Slice, with null where vtkValidPointMask is 0. The input must be non-composite image data; resample other datasets to an image first. For standard raster formats use pvWritePNGWriter, pvWriteTIFFWriter or pvWriteMetaImageWriter.
sources: ParaView 5.13.3 VTK/IO/Image/vtkJSONImageWriter.cxx:71-135 (arrays, ArrayName, Slice and valid-point mask)
pitfalls: ArrayName and Slice are honoured by the verifier: ArrayName must name a one-component point array (otherwise nothing is written and verification fails), and Slice must be -1 or below the image depth (a larger Slice is rejected with INVALID_SLICE before writing, because VTK does not bound-check it). Vector arrays and vtkValidPointMask are never written.
The writer prints values, origin and spacing with 6 significant digits (VTK vtkVariant::ToString precision 6), so floating-point data usually needs a positive tolerance.
Only pixels comparison is accepted and a custom readback reader is rejected for this writer.

pvWriteMetaImageWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer for MetaImage (.mhd): a short text header (dimensions, spacing, element type) plus a separate binary data file, the format read by ITK-based medical-imaging and segmentation tools. The input must be one non-composite vtkImageData; VTK writes the image scalars and compresses the data file by default. Schemaxis publishes it under the pixels contract: the file is read back and dimensions, component count and scalar values are compared, while coordinates and other fields are accepted as lost. Use pvWriteTIFFWriter or pvWritePNGWriter for 2-D raster interchange, or automatic VTK XML image output (.vti) to keep all arrays.
pitfalls: Only the image scalars are carried; make the array you need the active point scalars, or export VTK XML image data when several arrays matter.
Keep the header and its data file together when moving the result; the header refers to the data file by name.

pvWriteOpenVDBWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer for OpenVDB (.vdb), the sparse volume format used by Houdini, Blender and film-style renderers. It accepts non-composite image data (volumes) or point sets (meshes or point clouds handled through their points); with EnableColoring it adds a colour channel, and with EnableAlpha an alpha channel, computed from a lookup table supplied through the export's LookupTable resource. The declared publication uses the exact contract, comparing ParaView's readback of the .vdb with the input. EnableColoring needs a lookup table connected through resources (LookupTable) and the array to map named in ColorArrayName; otherwise no colour channel can be computed.

pvWritePNGWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer that stores image data (vtkImageData) as PNG, a lossless raster format holding 1 to 4 components of unsigned char (8-bit) or unsigned short (16-bit) values. It suits masks, label images and already-quantized images, not floating-point simulation fields; this writes data values, unlike a rendered scene image. Publication uses the pixels contract: the PNG is read back and its dimensions, components and values are compared with the input scalars. Use pvWriteTIFFWriter for 32-bit float data.
pitfalls: Float or double arrays are not supported; rescale and convert them to 8- or 16-bit integers upstream, because Schemaxis performs no implicit conversion.
Natively a 3-D image can be written as a numbered slice stack through a file pattern, but Schemaxis manages the file name, so export 2-D images.

pvWritePOBJWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer for Wavefront OBJ (.obj), a plain-text surface format read by almost every 3-D modelling, rendering and visualization tool. It writes the points, lines, triangles and polygons of polygonal data plus point normals and texture coordinates when present; solution fields are not stored. TextureFileName additionally writes a material (.mtl) file that refers to an existing texture image. Publication uses the geometry contract: the file is read back and the triangulated surface is compared, accepting loss of fields, point identity, interior cells and structure. Use pvWritePSTLWriter for triangle-only CAD or 3-D printing exchange, and VTK XML writers when fields matter.
pitfalls: Scalar and vector fields (pressure, velocity, ...) are lost; export a VTK XML format when the receiver needs them.
TextureFileName is written into the .mtl as given and the image is not copied into the output folder; use a path that still resolves where the OBJ will be opened.

pvWritePPLYWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer for Stanford PLY (.ply): polygonal surface geometry (points and polygons) for mesh, 3-D printing and point-cloud tools, binary by default (FileType). It accepts polygonal data only, so extract a surface first (pvExtractSurface). Field arrays are not carried, except optional per-point or per-cell RGB(A) colours written when EnableColoring is true, ColorArrayName names the array and a lookup-table resource is attached to the export. Publication uses the geometry contract: Schemaxis re-reads the file with ParaView's PLY reader and compares the triangulated surface within the tolerance.
pitfalls: Colours need all three: EnableColoring true, ColorArrayName and a LookupTable resource in the export's resources; otherwise the writer writes geometry only.
With ChooseArraysToWrite true, keep the colour array in the lists or no colours are written; the geometry comparison accepts the dropped fields, so array selection stays available here.

pvWritePSTLWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer for STL (.stl), the triangle-only surface format used by 3-D printing, CAD and meshing tools (for example as snappyHexMesh geometry). It writes binary STL by default or ASCII with FileType; only triangles are stored, with no units or fields. Publication uses the geometry contract: the file is re-read and its triangles are compared with the triangulated input surface within the tolerance, accepting loss of fields, point identity, interior cells and structure. Use pvWritePOBJWriter to keep polygons and normals, or pvWritePPLYWriter for per-vertex attributes.
sources: https://gitlab.kitware.com/vtk/vtk/-/raw/v9.3.0/IO/Geometry/vtkSTLWriter.cxx (WriteAsciiSTL and WriteBinarySTL triangulate polygons with npts > 3; lines and verts are not written)
pitfalls: Lines and vertex cells are not written to STL, so an input that contains them fails the geometry verification (Schemaxis compares the triangulated input, which keeps them); extract the surface (pvExtractSurface) and keep only polygons before exporting. Polygons with more than three vertices are triangulated by vtkSTLWriter itself; the ParaView help text about writing only their first three vertices is out of date.
Binary STL stores coordinates as 32-bit floats; give a small tolerance (the guide's example uses 0.000001) when the input uses double precision.
STL carries no length unit; check millimetres versus metres in the receiving tool.

pvWriteTIFFWriter.explanation: Explicit-export writer that saves image data (vtkImageData) as TIFF. vtkTIFFWriter accepts unsigned char, unsigned short or float scalars, so unlike PNG it can store 32-bit floating-point fields such as a sampled temperature image. Publication uses the pixels contract: the TIFF is read back and dimensions, components and values are compared; coordinates and other arrays are not preserved.
pitfalls: Double-precision and other integer types are rejected by the native writer; convert the array to float (or 8/16-bit unsigned) upstream.
Name the array in Scalars; otherwise ParaView decides which array is written.

pvXMLUniformGridAMRReader.explanation: Reads a VTK XML overlapping or non-overlapping AMR file (.vthb, or the older .vth): a hierarchy of refinement levels made of uniform-grid blocks, as written by AMR codes or by ParaView. The output is a vtkOverlappingAMR or vtkNonOverlappingAMR composite dataset. ParaView reads only DefaultNumberOfLevels levels unless a downstream filter asks for more, and its default is 1, so by default only the coarsest level is loaded. Use pvAMRGaussianPulseSource for a synthetic AMR test dataset.
pitfalls: Set DefaultNumberOfLevels to 0 (no limit) or to the number of levels you need; the ParaView default of 1 silently drops all refined levels.
On overlapping AMR, coarse cells under refined patches are blanked rather than removed; operations that ignore blanking count those regions twice.

pvXMLUnstructuredGridReader.explanation: Generated binding of ParaView's XML Unstructured Grid Reader: reads VTK XML unstructured grid files (.vtu) holding arbitrary cells (tetrahedra, hexahedra, polyhedra, mixed) with point and cell arrays, and outputs a vtkUnstructuredGrid. Unlike the curated readUnstructuredGrid (one file, every array), it accepts a list of files read as a time series and lets you choose which point and cell arrays to load. Use readParallelUnstructuredGrid for partitioned .pvtu output.
pitfalls: Use readUnstructuredGrid for the simple single-file case; it is the reader covered by Schemaxis's reader fixture.
With several files, time comes from each file's "TimeValue" field data when present (TimeArray), otherwise the step index; check the times before animating.
Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

pvXYZReader.explanation: Reads an XYZ molecular file (.xyz: atom count, comment line, then element symbol and x y z per atom) into a vtkMolecule; files with several consecutive frames become time steps. Bonds are not stored in the format; use pvComputeMoleculeBonds to derive them and pvMoleculeToLines to obtain polydata for general filters. Use pvPDBReader or pvCMLMoleculeReader for formats that carry more chemistry.
pitfalls: Coordinates are used as written (normally ångströms); nothing is converted.

Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

pvXdmf3ReaderS.explanation: Reads XDMF 3 files (.xmf/.xdmf) with heavy data in HDF5. A single domain with one grid gives that dataset type; otherwise the output is a multiblock. This variant treats a series of files as spatial partitions of one dataset (top-level partitioning) (AsTime false by default). Point and cell arrays and named sets can be selected. Use pvXdmf3ReaderT for the other file-series interpretation and pvXDMFReader for XDMF 2 files.
pitfalls: The HDF5 files must stay where the XML references them.
Array and set selections start from ParaView's choice; list them when later steps depend on particular names.
Schemaxis generates this reader binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check with a sample file of this format.

This variant treats a series of files as successive time steps (AsTime true by default). Point and cell arrays and named sets can be selected. Use pvXdmf3ReaderS for the other file-series interpretation and pvXDMFReader for XDMF 2 files.

Array and set selections start from ParaView's choice; list them when later steps depend on particular names.
