/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.explanation: How the neighbourhood (basis) of source points for each sample point is chosen. “Radius” uses every source point within Radius of the sample (VTK notes it has the better mathematical properties); “N Closest” uses the NumberOfPoints nearest source points regardless of distance, which always finds neighbours in sparse regions but may reach far away.
/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.label: Kernel footprint
/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from "Radius".
pitfalls: With “Radius”, a sample with no source point inside Radius is a null point, handled by the operation’s NullPointsStrategy (null value, mask or closest point). Increase Radius or use “N Closest” if many results are null.
A very large Radius makes every sample use huge neighbourhoods; VTK warns the cost can approach n³.

The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).

A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.

/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.explanation: Copies the values of a single source point from the neighbourhood: the most probable one when probability weights are supplied, otherwise the closest. ParaView’s point interpolators supply no probabilities, so here it behaves like Voronoi Kernel restricted to the footprint: the closest point within Radius (or among the N closest), and a null point when the radius is empty. Choose Voronoi Kernel for plain nearest-neighbour sampling.

/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.explanation: A runtime value replaces a literal setting with an expression that Schemaxis evaluates on each selected visit (one combination of simulation time and active axis values) before this setting is applied; $observe and $sample read upstream nodes after they have been updated on that visit. Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).
$observe and $sample make the named node a dependency, so it must be upstream; pointing back at this node or a consumer creates a cycle (PIPELINE_CYCLE).
A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.
In scene styles and cameras, $axis may only name an axis the scene's nodes already vary; use an explicit camera list for camera-only variation.
/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.label: Runtime value

/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.explanation: Exponent p in the weights 1/r^p. Larger p makes the nearest neighbours dominate (approaching nearest-neighbour behaviour); smaller p averages more evenly. p = 2 uses a fast squared-distance path; other values evaluate a power per neighbour and can be markedly slower.
/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.label: Power parameter
/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from 2.0.

/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.explanation: Nearest neighbour: each sample takes the values of the single closest source point (weight 1), with no radius limit, so an empty neighbourhood never produces a null point. It is fast and preserves original values without blending, but gives piecewise-constant, blocky fields. It is ParaView’s initial kernel for these interpolators; switch to Gaussian or Shepard for smooth fields.
pitfalls: When a sample is equally distant from several source points, one of them is chosen arbitrarily.

/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.explanation: Specify a point locator.

Bucket grid of the threaded locator that finds the source points around each sample point (for radius or N-closest searches). These settings affect speed and memory, not the interpolated values. Omitted settings keep ParaView’s initial values: automatic sizing with about 5 points per bucket.
/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.defaultMeaning: Omitted or {}: Schemaxis assigns none of these settings, so each keeps the native proxy’s initial value described on the individual setting.

Plane of sample points: a plane through Center with orientation Normal, limited to BoundingBox (inflated by Padding) and sampled where it crosses a regular grid set by RefinementMode with Resolution or CellSize. /$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.explanation: Axis-aligned region [xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax] that limits the plane: the output is the part of the plane inside this box (after Padding). The box is also the domain of the internal sampling grid, so a larger box at the same Resolution gives coarser spacing.
/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.label: Bounding box
/$defs/options-pvPointPlaneInterpolator/.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView chooses the initial value (its static default is [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1]; ParaView may instead derive it from the bounds of the input point cloud). Set it explicitly when the result depends on it.
pitfalls: Give each minimum before its maximum; an invalid box makes the source fail with “Invalid bounding box”.
If the plane through Center misses the box, the plane is empty and nothing is interpolated.

/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.explanation: Specify an interpolation kernel. By default a vtkVoronoiKernel is used (i.e., closest point). The interpolation kernel changes the basis of the interpolation.

Gaussian weighting whose shape is stretched or flattened along each source point’s normal, optionally scaled by a scalar (vtkEllipsoidalGaussianKernel). Choose it for oriented samples such as surface scans, where “pancake” splats aligned with the surface interpolate better than spheres. Without normals it reduces to a spherical Gaussian whose width is scaled by Eccentricity; plain Gaussian Kernel is cheaper in that case.

/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.explanation: Shape of the ellipsoid relative to each point’s normal: 1 is spherical, values below 1 give a needle along the normal, values above 1 a pancake perpendicular to it. In the weight exp(−Sharpness² · (r⊥²/E² + z²)/R²) it divides the distance measured perpendicular to the normal.
/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.label: Eccentricity
/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from 2.0.
pitfalls: Without normals (UseNormals false or no normals array) the perpendicular term applies in every direction, so Eccentricity simply widens (E > 1) or narrows (E < 1) a spherical Gaussian.

/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.explanation: Gaussian-weighted average of the neighbouring source points: weights exp(−(Sharpness · r / Radius)²), normalized to sum to 1; a source point exactly at the sample is copied. Gives smooth fields that favour nearby points; a good general choice. Shepard Kernel honours nearby values more sharply, Linear Kernel weights all neighbours equally, Voronoi Kernel copies the closest point, and Ellipsoidal Gaussian Kernel adds orientation from normals.

/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.explanation: Unweighted mean of the neighbouring source points: each point in the neighbourhood contributes equally, regardless of distance (a local box average). It smooths more than Shepard or Gaussian and does not reproduce the value at a source point that coincides with a sample unless that point is the only neighbour.

/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.explanation: How the neighbourhood (basis) of source points for each sample point is chosen. “Radius” uses every source point within Radius of the sample (VTK notes it has the better mathematical properties); “N Closest” uses the NumberOfPoints nearest source points regardless of distance, which always finds neighbours in sparse regions but may reach far away.
/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.label: Kernel footprint
/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from "Radius".
pitfalls: With “Radius”, a sample with no source point inside Radius is a null point, handled by the operation’s NullPointsStrategy (null value, mask or closest point). Increase Radius or use “N Closest” if many results are null.
A very large Radius makes every sample use huge neighbourhoods; VTK warns the cost can approach n³.

/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.explanation: Copies the values of a single source point from the neighbourhood: the most probable one when probability weights are supplied, otherwise the closest. ParaView’s point interpolators supply no probabilities, so here it behaves like Voronoi Kernel restricted to the footprint: the closest point within Radius (or among the N closest), and a null point when the radius is empty. Choose Voronoi Kernel for plain nearest-neighbour sampling.

/$defs/options-pvPointVolumeInterpolator.explanation: How output points that have no source point in their neighbourhood (null points) get a value. Mask Points adds an output array that marks each point valid (1) or null (0) and also sets the NullValue; Null Value (ParaView's default, entry 1) writes the NullValue to null points; Closest Point uses the closest source point. ParaView's own text calls Closest Point the default, but its XML default is 1 (Null Value), as in vtkPointInterpolator.
sources: ParaView 5.13.3 VTKExtensions/Points/Resources/points.xml:1003-1023 (NullPointsStrategy default_values "1" = Null Value; text names ClosestPoint)

/$defs/options-pvPrincipalComponentAnaly.explanation:
When reporting assessments, should the full eigenvector decomposition be used to project the original vector into the new space (Full basis), or should a fixed subset of the decomposition be used (Fixed-size basis), or should the projection be clipped to preserve at least some fixed "energy" (Fixed-energy basis)?

As an example, suppose the variables of interest were {A,B,C,D,E} and that the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix for these were {5,2,1.5,1,.5}. If the "Full basis" scheme is used, then all 5 components of the eigenvectors will be used to project each {A,B,C,D,E}-tuple in the original data into a new 5-components space.

If the "Fixed-size" scheme is used and the "Basis Size" property is set to 4, then only the first 4 eigenvector components will be used to project each {A,B,C,D,E}-tuple into the new space and that space will be of dimension 4, not 5.

If the "Fixed-energy basis" scheme is used and the "Basis Energy" property is set to 0.8, then only the first 3 eigenvector components will be used to project each {A,B,C,D,E}-tuple into the new space, which will be of dimension 3. The number 3 is chosen because 3 is the lowest N for which the sum of the first N eigenvalues divided by the sum of all eigenvalues is larger than the specified "Basis Energy" (i.e., (5+2+1.5)/10 = 0.85 > 0.8).
/$defs/options-pvPrincipalComponentAnaly.label: Basis Scheme

/$defs/options-pvPrincipalComponentAnaly.explanation:
When reporting assessments, should the full eigenvector decomposition be used to project the original vector into the new space (Full basis), or should a fixed subset of the decomposition be used (Fixed-size basis), or should the projection be clipped to preserve at least some fixed "energy" (Fixed-energy basis)?

As an example, suppose the variables of interest were {A,B,C,D,E} and that the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix for these were {5,2,1.5,1,.5}. If the "Full basis" scheme is used, then all 5 components of the eigenvectors will be used to project each {A,B,C,D,E}-tuple in the original data into a new 5-components space.

If the "Fixed-size" scheme is used and the "Basis Size" property is set to 4, then only the first 4 eigenvector components will be used to project each {A,B,C,D,E}-tuple into the new space and that space will be of dimension 4, not 5.

If the "Fixed-energy basis" scheme is used and the "Basis Energy" property is set to 0.8, then only the first 3 eigenvector components will be used to project each {A,B,C,D,E}-tuple into the new space, which will be of dimension 3. The number 3 is chosen because 3 is the lowest N for which the sum of the first N eigenvalues divided by the sum of all eigenvalues is larger than the specified "Basis Energy" (i.e., (5+2+1.5)/10 = 0.85 > 0.8).

/$defs/options-pvPrincipalComponentAnaly.explanation:
Specify the task to be performed: modeling and/or assessment.
  1. "Detailed model of input data," creates a set of output tables containing a calculated statistical model of the entire input dataset;
  2. "Model a subset of the data," creates an output table (or tables) summarizing a randomly-chosen subset of the input dataset;
  3. "Assess the data with a model," adds attributes to the first input dataset using a model provided on the second input port; and
  4. "Model and assess the same data," is really just operations 2 and 3 above applied to the same input dataset. The model is first trained using a fraction of the input data and then the entire dataset is assessed using that model.
When the task includes creating a model (i.e., tasks 2, and 4), you may adjust the fraction of the input dataset used for training. You should avoid using a large fraction of the input data for training as you will then not be able to detect overfitting. The Training fraction setting will be ignored for tasks 1 and 3.
/$defs/options-pvPrincipalComponentAnaly.label: Task

Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).
$observe and $sample make the named node a dependency, so it must be upstream; pointing back at this node or a consumer creates a cycle (PIPELINE_CYCLE).
A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.

/$defs/options-pvRedistributeDataSet.explanation: Settings: BoundaryMode (ParaView default Assign to one region), NumberOfPartitions (default -1, one per MPI process), LoadBalanceAcrossAllBlocks (default true), PreservePartitionsInOutput (default false), GenerateGlobalCellIds (default false) and EnableDebugging (default false; keeps helper arrays).

/$defs/options-pvRedistributeDataSet/pro.explanation: This property determines how cells that lie on processor boundaries are handled. The "Assign to one region" option assigns each boundary cell to exactly one process, which is useful for isosurfacing. Selecting "Assign to all regions" causes the cells on the boundaries to be copied to each process that shares that boundary. The "Split cells" option breaks cells across process boundary lines so that pieces of the cell lie in different processes. This option is useful for volume rendering.
/$defs/options-pvRedistributeDataSet/pro.label: Boundary Mode

/$defs/options-pvRedistributeDataSet/pro.explanation: This property determines how cells that lie on processor boundaries are handled. The "Assign to one region" option assigns each boundary cell to exactly one process, which is useful for isosurfacing. Selecting "Assign to all regions" causes the cells on the boundaries to be copied to each process that shares that boundary. The "Split cells" option breaks cells across process boundary lines so that pieces of the cell lie in different processes. This option is useful for volume rendering.

A runtime value replaces a literal setting with an expression that Schemaxis evaluates on each selected visit (one combination of simulation time and active axis values) before this setting is applied; $observe and $sample read upstream nodes after they have been updated on that visit. Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).

/$defs/options-pvReductionFilter/propert.explanation: Where the gathered result ends up. In this proxy's XML the first two labels are swapped relative to VTK: "Move all data to one processor" sets native value 0, which vtkReductionFilter defines as REDUCE_ALL_TO_ONE (the target process holds the result while the others keep their own data), and "Reduce all data to one processor" sets value 1, MOVE_ALL_TO_ONE (the other processes end with no data). "Reduce all data to all processors" gives every process the full result, at the highest memory cost. In a serial run all three give the same result.
/$defs/options-pvReductionFilter/propert.label: Reduction mode
/$defs/options-pvReductionFilter/propert.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from "Move all data to one processor" (native value 0, REDUCE_ALL_TO_ONE).
examples: Reduce all data to all processors
pitfalls: Choose by the behaviour you need, not by the label; pvAppendReduce uses the VTK-consistent labelling for the same values.

Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).
$observe and $sample make the named node a dependency, so it must be upstream; pointing back at this node or a consumer creates a cycle (PIPELINE_CYCLE).
A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.
In scene styles and cameras, $axis may only name an axis the scene's nodes already vary; use an explicit camera list for camera-only variation.
/$defs/options-pvResampleAMR/properties/.label: Runtime value

/$defs/options-pvResampleToImage.explanation: UseInputBounds (ParaView default true) makes the image span the input's bounding box; set it false to use SamplingBounds. SamplingDimensions (default [100, 100, 100]) gives sample points per axis, so spacing = (max − min) / (dimension − 1).

/$defs/options-pvResampleToImage/propert.explanation: One bound of the sampling box, in the order [xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax]; the first and last image points lie exactly on the bounds. Used only when UseInputBounds is false.
/$defs/options-pvResampleToImage/propert.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView chooses the initial value (its static default is [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1]; ParaView may instead use the input bounds). Set it explicitly together with UseInputBounds false.
pitfalls: Giving [xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax] is a common mistake; the order alternates minimum and maximum per axis.

/$defs/options-pvResampleToLine/properti.explanation: When dealing with composite datasets, partial arrays are common i.e. data-arrays that are not available in all of the blocks. By default, this filter only passes those point and cell data-arrays that are available in all the blocks i.e. partial arrays are removed. When PassPartialArrays is turned on, this behavior is changed to take a union of all arrays present thus partial arrays are passed as well. However, for composite dataset input, this filter still produces a non-composite output. For all those locations in a block of where a particular data array is missing, this filter uses vtkMath::Nan() for double and float arrays, and 0 for all other types of arrays i.e int, char etc.
/$defs/options-pvResampleToLine/properti.label: Pass Partial Arrays

/$defs/options-pvResampleToLine/properti.explanation: This property controls the coordinates of the first endpoint of the line.
One coordinate (x, y, then z) of the first endpoint of the sampling line, in the input's coordinate units. arc_length is measured from Point1, so swapping the endpoints reverses the plot direction.
sources: evidence/2026-10-10-guidance-completion/defects/probes/probe_creation.py (PlotOverLine, ResampleToLine) (bounded native probe, 2026-10-12, ParaView 5.13.3 pvbatch, serial)
/$defs/options-pvResampleToLine/properti.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; never the static [0, 0, 0]. In a bounded native probe with a polydata upstream, an omitted Point1 read back as (1, 1, 1) when the node was created before its upstream had data, which is what a Schemaxis batch run does, a point unrelated to the data (composite inputs give other uninitialised-bounds corners, by the source); with data already present it was the minimum corner of the input's bounding box. Set both endpoints.

One coordinate (x, y, then z) of the second endpoint of the sampling line, in the input's coordinate units. arc_length is measured from Point1, so swapping the endpoints reverses the plot direction.
sources: evidence/2026-10-10-guidance-completion/defects/probes/probe_creation.py (PlotOverLine, ResampleToLine) (bounded native probe, 2026-10-12, ParaView 5.13.3 pvbatch, serial)
/$defs/options-pvResampleToLine/properti.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; never the static [0, 0, 0]. In a bounded native probe with a polydata upstream, an omitted Point2 read back as (-1, -1, -1) when the node was created before its upstream had data, which is what a Schemaxis batch run does, a point unrelated to the data (composite inputs give other uninitialised-bounds corners, by the source); with data already present it was the maximum corner of the input's bounding box. Set both endpoints.

/$defs/options-pvResampleToLine/properti.explanation: A runtime value replaces a literal setting with an expression that Schemaxis evaluates on each selected visit (one combination of simulation time and active axis values) before this setting is applied; $observe and $sample read upstream nodes after they have been updated on that visit. Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).
$observe and $sample make the named node a dependency, so it must be upstream; pointing back at this node or a consumer creates a cycle (PIPELINE_CYCLE).
A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.
In scene styles and cameras, $axis may only name an axis the scene's nodes already vary; use an explicit camera list for camera-only variation.

/$defs/options-pvResampleToLine/properti.explanation: How sample points are placed on the line. Sample Uniformly spaces Resolution samples evenly, which smooths over cell structure; Sample At Cell Boundaries puts a pair of points at every cell crossing so cell data appear as exact steps (most faithful); Sample At Segment Centers gives one sample per crossed cell, convenient for cell-wise tables.
/$defs/options-pvResampleToLine/properti.label: Sampling pattern
/$defs/options-pvResampleToLine/properti.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from Sample Uniformly.
pitfalls: Resolution is used only with Sample Uniformly; the other patterns take their point count from the mesh.

/$defs/options-pvResampleWithDataset/pro.explanation: The cell locator to use for finding cells for probing.
/$defs/options-pvResampleWithDataset/pro.label: Cell Locator

/$defs/options-pvResampleWithDataset/pro.explanation: The cell locator to use for finding cells for probing.

Classic VTK cell locator: a uniform-level octree whose leaf buckets list the cells they overlap. A general-purpose, single-threaded choice; use it to reproduce older VTK behaviour. For large meshes the threaded Static Cell Locator, ParaView’s initial choice here, is normally faster.
pitfalls: All locators answer the same question (which source cell contains each sample point); the choice is about speed and memory, not about how values are interpolated.

A runtime value replaces a literal setting with an expression that Schemaxis evaluates on each selected visit (one combination of simulation time and active axis values) before this setting is applied; $observe and $sample read upstream nodes after they have been updated on that visit. pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).

/$defs/options-pvResourcePVLookupTable/p.explanation: The color space used for interpolation: RGB, HSV, Lab (CIELAB), or Diverging. In HSV mode, if HSVWrap is on, it will take the shortest path in Hue (going back through 0 if that is the shortest way around the hue circle) whereas if HSVWrap is off it will not go through 0 (in order the match the current functionality of vtkLookupTable). Diverging is a special mode where colors will pass through white when interpolating between two saturated colors. In Lab/CIEDE2000 mode, it will take the shortest path in the Lab color space with respect to the CIE Delta E 2000 color distance measure. In Step mode, the color of an interval is the color of the second point of the interval.

A runtime value replaces a literal setting with an expression that Schemaxis evaluates on each selected visit (one combination of simulation time and active axis values) before this setting is applied; $observe and $sample read upstream nodes after they have been updated on that visit. Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).
$observe and $sample make the named node a dependency, so it must be upstream; pointing back at this node or a consumer creates a cycle (PIPELINE_CYCLE).
A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.
In scene styles and cameras, $axis may only name an axis the scene's nodes already vary; use an explicit camera list for camera-only variation.
/$defs/options-pvResourcePVLookupTable/p.label: Runtime value

/$defs/options-pvResourcePiecewiseFuncti.explanation: Points defines the function; AllowDuplicateScalars allows vertical steps and UseLogScale interpolates in log space. Omitted settings keep ParaView's XML defaults: a linear ramp from 0 at x = 0 to 1 at x = 1.

/$defs/options-pvResourcePiecewiseFuncti.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from true (VTK's own default is false).

/$defs/options-pvResourcePiecewiseFuncti.explanation: Control points as a flat list of [x, y, midpoint, sharpness] groups: x is the data value, y the function value there (usually opacity 0 to 1), midpoint (0 to 1) where between this point and the next the value is halfway, and sharpness from 0 (linear) to 1 (step). Give groups in increasing x.
/$defs/options-pvResourcePiecewiseFuncti.label: Control points
/$defs/options-pvResourcePiecewiseFuncti.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from [0, 0, 0.5, 0, 1, 1, 0.5, 0], a linear ramp from 0 at x = 0 to 1 at x = 1.
pitfalls: The length must be a multiple of 4; Schemaxis rejects incomplete groups.
Use midpoint 0.5 and sharpness 0 for plain linear interpolation.

/$defs/options-pvResourceTransferFunctio.explanation: Range sets the x and y extents, Boxes adds coloured rectangles, OutputDimensions the size of the sampled image, and AutomaticRescaleRangeMode how ParaView views would rescale it. Omitted settings keep ParaView's XML defaults: range [0, 1, 0, 1], no boxes, a 10 x 10 image.

Choose whether and how to automatically rescale the color map range. "Never" means the color map range will never be changed. "Grow and update on 'Apply'" will expand the range to contain the union of the current range and the range of the current data source. "Grow and update every timestep" will expand the range to contain the union of the current range and the range of the current data source when the timestep is changed. "Clamp and update every timestep" will update the color map range to the current source data range.
/$defs/options-pvResourceTransferFunctio.label: Automatic Rescale Range Mode

These are a list of 8-tuples of the form (x, y, width, height, r, g, b, a) where (x, y) is the position i.e. the range-min of the box, (width, height) specify the dimensions of the box in the scalar units and (r, g, b, a) denote the color with maximum alpha of the box. The color and alpha components are in the range [0, 1].

One number of the flat Boxes list, read in [x, y, width, height, red, green, blue, alpha] groups of eight: (x, y) is the box's lower corner and width and height its size, in the data units of Range; the colour and maximum alpha are from 0 to 1.
pitfalls: The list length must be a multiple of 8; boxes outside Range do not appear.

/$defs/options-pvRestartedSimExodusReade.explanation: Settings choose the file(s) (required), which blocks, sets and maps are loaded and which variables are read on each, how displacements and mode shapes are applied, and which id arrays are generated. VTK's Exodus reader starts with element blocks and the first map of each kind enabled but edge and face blocks, sets and all result variables disabled; other omitted settings keep ParaView's values (e.g. ApplyDisplacements true, DisplacementMagnitude 1).

If this flag is on and HasModeShapes is also on, then this reader will report a continuous time range [0,1] and animate the displacements in a periodic sinusoid. If this flag is off and HasModeShapes is on, this reader ignores time. This flag has no effect if HasModeShapes is off.
/$defs/options-pvRestartedSimExodusReade.label: Animate Vibrations

/$defs/options-pvRestartedSimExodusReade.explanation: If this flag is on and HasModeShapes is also on, then this reader will report a continuous time range [0,1] and animate the displacements in a periodic sinusoid. Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).
$observe and $sample make the named node a dependency, so it must be upstream; pointing back at this node or a consumer creates a cycle (PIPELINE_CYCLE).
A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.
In scene styles and cameras, $axis may only name an axis the scene's nodes already vary; use an explicit camera list for camera-only variation.

A runtime value replaces a literal setting with an expression that Schemaxis evaluates on each selected visit (one combination of simulation time and active axis values) before this setting is applied; $observe and $sample read upstream nodes after they have been updated on that visit. Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).

/$defs/options-pvRotationalExtrusion/pro.explanation: If this property is set to 1, the open ends of the swept surface will be capped with a copy of the input dataset. This works property if the input is a 2D surface composed of filled polygons. If the input dataset is a closed solid (e.g., a sphere), then either two copies of the dataset will be drawn or no surface will be drawn. No surface is drawn if either this property is set to 0 or if the two surfaces would occupy exactly the same 3D space (i.e., the Angle property's value is a multiple of 360, and the values of the Translation and DeltaRadius properties are 0).

/$defs/options-pvSLACDataReader.explanation: Settings choose the mesh file (required) and the optional mode files, whether the external surface (ParaView default true) and the internal volume (default false) are read, whether surface midpoints build quadratic triangles (ParaView 5.13.3 default false) and, for oscillating modes, a per-mode amplitude factor and phase shift. /$defs/options-pvSLACDataReader/properti.explanation: Sets the scale factor for each mode. By default, each scale factor is set to 1.
/$defs/options-pvSLACDataReader/properti.label: Frequency Scale

/$defs/options-pvSLACDataReader/properti.explanation: Sets the scale factor for each mode. By default, each scale factor is set to 1.

Amplitude factor for one mode, by position: the first element applies to the first mode file, the second to the second, and so on. For oscillating (frequency) modes each mode's field magnitude is multiplied by its factor before the modes are summed, so the factors set the relative weight of superposed modes.
/$defs/options-pvSLACDataReader/properti.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; every mode starts with factor 1 (ParaView documentation and vtkSLACReader).
pitfalls: The factor is used only for mode files that store a frequency; time-series mode files are read as stored.

/$defs/options-pvSLACDataReader/properti.explanation: Sets the phase offset for each mode. By default, shift is set to 0.

Phase offset added to one mode, by position (first element for the first mode file, and so on). The reader evaluates each oscillating mode as cos(initial phase + 2πft + shift), so a shift moves that mode within its cycle, e.g. to align superposed modes.
/$defs/options-pvSLACDataReader/properti.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; every mode starts with shift 0.
pitfalls: Degrees are not converted: a quarter period is 1.5708, not 90.

/$defs/options-pvSLACDataReader/properti.explanation: A runtime value replaces a literal setting with an expression that Schemaxis evaluates on each selected visit (one combination of simulation time and active axis values) before this setting is applied; $observe and $sample read upstream nodes after they have been updated on that visit. Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).
$observe and $sample make the named node a dependency, so it must be upstream; pointing back at this node or a consumer creates a cycle (PIPELINE_CYCLE).
A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.
In scene styles and cameras, $axis may only name an axis the scene's nodes already vary; use an explicit camera list for camera-only variation.
/$defs/options-pvSLACDataReader/properti.label: Runtime value

/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator.explanation: Settings choose the SPH kernel (and through its options the smoothing length and dimension), the particle arrays used for density, mass, exclusion and derivatives, null-point handling, Shepard-sum output, the locator and pass-through of the probe structure's own arrays. Omitted settings keep ParaView's values: SPH Quintic kernel with spatial step 0.0001 and dimension 3, density array Rho, Null Value strategy with value 0, and a Shepard Summation array computed. CutoffArray can give a per-point neighbourhood radius instead of the kernel cutoff.

/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.explanation: Indicate whether to compute the summation of Shepard coefficients. In the interior of a SPH point cloud, the Shephard summation value should be ~1.0. Towards the boundary, the Shepard summation is less than 1.0. If ComputeShepardSum is specified, then the output will contain an array of summed Shepard weights for each output point.
/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.label: Compute Shepard Sum

/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.explanation: Smoothing kernel W(r, h) used to weight neighbouring particles, following D.J. Price's SPH formulations. All four take the kernel options SpatialStep (the smoothing length h, in dataset units) and Dimension (1 to 3, the dimension of the particle problem, which sets the normalization). They differ in order and support radius: SPH Cubic Kernel (cutoff 2h, cheapest and least smooth), SPH Quartic Kernel (2.5h), SPH Quintic Kernel (3h, higher order, the ParaView default) and SPH Wendland Quintic Kernel (2h, a compactly supported Wendland function). Pick the kernel your SPH solver used so interpolated values are consistent with the simulation.
/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.label: SPH kernel
/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 selects SPH Quintic Kernel (the ProxyListDomain default) with its own SpatialStep 0.0001 and Dimension 3.
pitfalls: Leaving SpatialStep at 0.0001 for real particle spacing gives empty neighbourhoods and null values; set it to the solver's smoothing length.
Dimension must match the particle problem (2 for a 2-D simulation), otherwise the kernel normalization and hence the interpolated magnitudes are wrong.

/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.explanation: Cubic spline SPH kernel after D. J. Price (2012), with support radius 2 × SpatialStep: the classic spline kernel, with the smallest neighbourhood of the three spline kernels. Choose the kernel used by the simulation that produced the particles so that interpolated fields match the solver’s own estimates.
pitfalls: SPH interpolation also needs the operation’s DensityArray (ParaView expects one; its static name is “Rho”). Add MassArray for true particle volumes; without it the volume falls back to SpatialStep^Dimension.

/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.explanation: Smoothing length (SpatialStep) and dimension of the SPH kernel. SpatialStep must match the particle spacing; omitted settings keep ParaView’s initial values (SpatialStep 0.0001, Dimension 3), which rarely suit real data.
/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.defaultMeaning: Omitted or {}: Schemaxis assigns none of these settings, so each keeps the native proxy’s initial value described on the individual setting.

/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.explanation: Spatial dimension of the particle data (1, 2 or 3). It selects the kernel’s normalization constant and the power of SpatialStep used for the default particle volume (SpatialStep^Dimension). Use 2 for planar simulations and 3 for volumetric ones.
/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.label: Dimension
/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from 3.
pitfalls: Interpolating 3D particles with Dimension 2 (or vice versa) mis-scales every result.

/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.explanation: Spatial dimension of the particle data (1, 2 or 3). It selects the kernel’s normalization constant and the power of SpatialStep used for the default particle volume (SpatialStep^Dimension). Use 2 for planar simulations and 3 for volumetric ones.

/$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.explanation: Smoothing length h of the kernel in dataset units. Neighbours are gathered within 2 × h of each sample (unless the operation supplies a cutoff array), weights are normalized by h^Dimension, and without a mass array each particle’s volume is taken as h^Dimension. /$defs/options-pvSPHDatasetInterpolator/.explanation: Specify a strategy to use when encountering a "null" point during the interpolation process. Null points occur when the local neighborhood (of nearby points to interpolate from) is empty. If the strategy is set to MaskPoints, then an output array is created that marks points as being valid (=1) or null (invalid =0) (and the NullValue is set as well). If the strategy is set to NullValue, then the output data value(s) are set to the NullPoint value (specified in the output point data).

/$defs/options-pvSPHLineInterpolator.explanation: Source settings define the probe geometry. Settings choose the SPH kernel (and through its options the smoothing length and dimension), the particle arrays used for density, mass, exclusion and derivatives, null-point handling, Shepard-sum output, the locator and pass-through of the probe structure's own arrays. Omitted settings keep ParaView's values: SPH Quintic kernel with spatial step 0.0001 and dimension 3, density array Rho, Null Value strategy with value 0, and a Shepard Summation array computed.

If ComputeShepardSum is specified, then the output will contain an array of summed Shepard weights for each output point.

/$defs/options-pvSPHLineInterpolator/pro.explanation: Smoothing kernel W(r, h) used to weight neighbouring particles, following D.J. Price's SPH formulations. All four take the kernel options SpatialStep (the smoothing length h, in dataset units) and Dimension (1 to 3, the dimension of the particle problem, which sets the normalization). They differ in order and support radius: SPH Cubic Kernel (cutoff 2h, cheapest and least smooth), SPH Quartic Kernel (2.5h), SPH Quintic Kernel (3h, higher order, the ParaView default) and SPH Wendland Quintic Kernel (2h, a compactly supported Wendland function). Pick the kernel your SPH solver used so interpolated values are consistent with the simulation.
/$defs/options-pvSPHLineInterpolator/pro.label: SPH kernel
/$defs/options-pvSPHLineInterpolator/pro.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 selects SPH Quintic Kernel (the ProxyListDomain default) with its own SpatialStep 0.0001 and Dimension 3.
pitfalls: Leaving SpatialStep at 0.0001 for real particle spacing gives empty neighbourhoods and null values; set it to the solver's smoothing length.
Dimension must match the particle problem (2 for a 2-D simulation), otherwise the kernel normalization and hence the interpolated magnitudes are wrong.

/$defs/options-pvSPHLineInterpolator/pro.explanation: Cubic spline SPH kernel after D. J. Price (2012), with support radius 2 × SpatialStep: the classic spline kernel, with the smallest neighbourhood of the three spline kernels. Choose the kernel used by the simulation that produced the particles so that interpolated fields match the solver’s own estimates.
pitfalls: SPH interpolation also needs the operation’s DensityArray (ParaView expects one; its static name is “Rho”). Add MassArray for true particle volumes; without it the volume falls back to SpatialStep^Dimension.

/$defs/options-pvSPHLineInterpolator/pro.explanation: Smoothing length h of the kernel in dataset units. /$defs/options-pvSPHLineInterpolator/pro.explanation: Specify a strategy to use when encountering a "null" point during the interpolation process. Null points occur when the local neighborhood (of nearby points to interpolate from) is empty. If the strategy is set to MaskPoints, then an output array is created that marks points as being valid (=1) or null (invalid =0) (and the NullValue is set as well). If the strategy is set to NullValue, then the output data value(s) are set to the NullPoint value (specified in the output point data).

/$defs/options-pvSPHPlaneInterpolator.explanation: Source settings define the probe geometry. Settings choose the SPH kernel (and through its options the smoothing length and dimension), the particle arrays used for density, mass, exclusion and derivatives, null-point handling, Shepard-sum output, the locator and pass-through of the probe structure's own arrays. Omitted settings keep ParaView's values: SPH Quintic kernel with spatial step 0.0001 and dimension 3, density array Rho, Null Value strategy with value 0, and a Shepard Summation array computed.

/$defs/options-pvSPHPlaneInterpolator/pr.explanation: Indicate whether to compute the summation of Shepard coefficients. In the interior of a SPH point cloud, the Shephard summation value should be ~1.0. Towards the boundary, the Shepard summation is less than 1.0. If ComputeShepardSum is specified, then the output will contain an array of summed Shepard weights for each output point.
/$defs/options-pvSPHPlaneInterpolator/pr.label: Compute Shepard Sum

/$defs/options-pvSPHPlaneInterpolator/pr.explanation: Indicate whether to compute the summation of Shepard coefficients. In the interior of a SPH point cloud, the Shephard summation value should be ~1.0. Towards the boundary, the Shepard summation is less than 1.0. If ComputeShepardSum is specified, then the output will contain an array of summed Shepard weights for each output point.

/$defs/options-pvSPHPlaneInterpolator/pr.explanation: Smoothing kernel W(r, h) used to weight neighbouring particles, following D.J. Price's SPH formulations. All four take the kernel options SpatialStep (the smoothing length h, in dataset units) and Dimension (1 to 3, the dimension of the particle problem, which sets the normalization). They differ in order and support radius: SPH Cubic Kernel (cutoff 2h, cheapest and least smooth), SPH Quartic Kernel (2.5h), SPH Quintic Kernel (3h, higher order, the ParaView default) and SPH Wendland Quintic Kernel (2h, a compactly supported Wendland function). Pick the kernel your SPH solver used so interpolated values are consistent with the simulation.
/$defs/options-pvSPHPlaneInterpolator/pr.label: SPH kernel
/$defs/options-pvSPHPlaneInterpolator/pr.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 selects SPH Quintic Kernel (the ProxyListDomain default) with its own SpatialStep 0.0001 and Dimension 3.
pitfalls: Leaving SpatialStep at 0.0001 for real particle spacing gives empty neighbourhoods and null values; set it to the solver's smoothing length.
Dimension must match the particle problem (2 for a 2-D simulation), otherwise the kernel normalization and hence the interpolated magnitudes are wrong.

/$defs/options-pvSPHPlaneInterpolator/pr.explanation: Cubic spline SPH kernel after D. J. /$defs/options-pvSPHPlaneInterpolator/pr.explanation: Quintic spline SPH kernel after D. J. Price (2012), with support radius 3 × SpatialStep, the widest neighbourhood of the four, and ParaView’s initial SPH kernel. /$defs/options-pvSPHVolumeInterpolator.explanation: Source settings define the probe geometry. Settings choose the SPH kernel (and through its options the smoothing length and dimension), the particle arrays used for density, mass, exclusion and derivatives, null-point handling, Shepard-sum output, the locator and pass-through of the probe structure's own arrays. Omitted settings keep ParaView's values: SPH Quintic kernel with spatial step 0.0001 and dimension 3, density array Rho, Null Value strategy with value 0, and a Shepard Summation array computed.

/$defs/options-pvSPHVolumeInterpolator/p.explanation: Indicate whether to compute the summation of Shepard coefficients. In the interior of a SPH point cloud, the Shephard summation value should be ~1.0. Towards the boundary, the Shepard summation is less than 1.0. If ComputeShepardSum is specified, then the output will contain an array of summed Shepard weights for each output point.
/$defs/options-pvSPHVolumeInterpolator/p.label: Compute Shepard Sum

/$defs/options-pvSPHVolumeInterpolator/p.explanation: Smoothing kernel W(r, h) used to weight neighbouring particles, following D.J. Price's SPH formulations. All four take the kernel options SpatialStep (the smoothing length h, in dataset units) and Dimension (1 to 3, the dimension of the particle problem, which sets the normalization). They differ in order and support radius: SPH Cubic Kernel (cutoff 2h, cheapest and least smooth), SPH Quartic Kernel (2.5h), SPH Quintic Kernel (3h, higher order, the ParaView default) and SPH Wendland Quintic Kernel (2h, a compactly supported Wendland function). Pick the kernel your SPH solver used so interpolated values are consistent with the simulation.
/$defs/options-pvSPHVolumeInterpolator/p.label: SPH kernel
/$defs/options-pvSPHVolumeInterpolator/p.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 selects SPH Quintic Kernel (the ProxyListDomain default) with its own SpatialStep 0.0001 and Dimension 3.
pitfalls: Leaving SpatialStep at 0.0001 for real particle spacing gives empty neighbourhoods and null values; set it to the solver's smoothing length.
Dimension must match the particle problem (2 for a 2-D simulation), otherwise the kernel normalization and hence the interpolated magnitudes are wrong.

/$defs/options-pvSPHVolumeInterpolator/p.explanation: Specify a strategy to use when encountering a "null" point during the interpolation process. Null points occur when the local neighborhood (of nearby points to interpolate from) is empty. If the strategy is set to MaskPoints, then an output array is created that marks points as being valid (=1) or null (invalid =0) (and the NullValue is set as well). If the strategy is set to NullValue, then the output data value(s) are set to the NullPoint value (specified in the output point data).
/$defs/options-pvSPHVolumeInterpolator/p.label: Null Points Strategy

/$defs/options-pvSTEPReader/properties/F.explanation: Path of one STEP file (.step, .stp). Further entries are read as a file series, one time step per file in the order listed, not as an assembly; to combine parts, read each in its own node and use append. Relative paths are resolved from the working directory of the Schemaxis process (in Studio, the directory it was launched from), not from the JSON file's folder. The value must be a constant because file names are passed when the reader is created.
sources: https://gitlab.kitware.com/paraview/paraview/-/raw/v5.13.3/VTKExtensions/IOCore/vtkFileSeriesReader.h (files are read in the order they are added)

/$defs/options-pvSTLReader/properties/Fi.label: File Names

/$defs/options-pvSTLReader/properties/Fi.explanation: Path of one STL file. Several entries form a time series in list order: if the first file reports no time, entry k is given time k (zero-based); otherwise each file's own times are used.

/$defs/options-pvSegYReader/properties/V.explanation: Specify whether the vertical coordinates in the SEG-Y file are heights (positive up) or depths (positive down). /$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.explanation: When true, ParaView replaces Normal by the coordinate axis of its largest absolute component, so the plane is always perpendicular to x, y or z. The snapped normal is always positive ([-1, 0, 0] becomes [1, 0, 0]), and tied components are all set to 1 ([1, 1, 0] stays [1, 1, 0]) rather than resolved to one axis. When false, Normal is used as given.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.label: Always snap to nearest axis
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from true.
pitfalls: The snap is applied when Normal is set and is not undone when snapping is later turned off (SetAxisAligned re-applies the stored, already snapped normal). For an oblique plane, use the Plane choice where the operation offers it.
ParaView keeps the requested Normal in the property while the plane uses the snapped vector, so Schemaxis readback does not reveal the snap; write a pure axis normal such as [0, 0, 1].

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.explanation: Direction perpendicular to the plane, [nx, ny, nz]. It orients the plane and defines its positive side: points toward which the normal points have positive implicit-function values Normal·(x − Origin), points on the other side negative; clip and extract operations use this sign to decide which side to keep. VTK does not normalize the vector, so its length scales the function value.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.explanation: A runtime value replaces a literal setting with an expression that Schemaxis evaluates on each selected visit (one combination of simulation time and active axis values) before this setting is applied; $observe and $sample read upstream nodes after they have been updated on that visit. Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).
$observe and $sample make the named node a dependency, so it must be upstream; pointing back at this node or a consumer creates a cycle (PIPELINE_CYCLE).
A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.
In scene styles and cameras, $axis may only name an axis the scene's nodes already vary; use an explicit camera list for camera-only variation.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.label: Runtime value

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.explanation: A point the plane passes through, as [x, y, z] in the input’s own coordinates. With Normal it defines the infinite plane Normal·(x − Origin) = 0 used to clip, slice, cut or select. Moving Origin along the normal shifts the plane; moving it within the plane changes nothing.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.label: Origin
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView chooses the initial value (its static default is [0, 0, 0]; ParaView may instead derive it from the centre of the input’s bounding box). Set it explicitly when the result depends on it.
pitfalls: Coordinates are absolute, not fractions of the model: on a part spanning 0–2000 mm, [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] lies at a corner. Use the model’s own units.
Offset is added on top of Origin along Normal; keep Offset at 0 if Origin should be the exact plane position.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.explanation: An infinite flat plane through Origin, oriented by Normal (ParaView’s vtkPVPlane). It is the usual choice, and ParaView’s initial one for most operations that offer it: use it for planar cuts, clips or selections at any orientation. Where offered, prefer Axis Aligned Plane when the plane must stay exactly perpendicular to x, y or z, and Box, Sphere or Cylinder when the region of interest is closed or curved.
pitfalls: The plane is unbounded: it cuts through every part of the dataset it crosses, including distant parts.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.explanation: Position and orientation of the plane: Origin (a point on it), Normal (its orientation and positive side) and Offset (an extra shift along the normal). Origin and Normal decide the result; omitted settings keep ParaView’s initial values, and Origin may be derived from the input bounds, so set both explicitly for reproducible results.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.defaultMeaning: Omitted or {}: Schemaxis assigns none of these settings, so each keeps the native proxy’s initial value described on the individual setting.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.explanation: Position and orientation of the plane: Origin (a point on it), Normal (its orientation and positive side) and Offset (an extra shift along the normal). Origin and Normal decide the result; omitted settings keep ParaView’s initial values, and Origin may be derived from the input bounds, so set both explicitly for reproducible results.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.defaultMeaning: Omitted or {}: Schemaxis assigns none of these settings, so each keeps the native proxy’s initial value described on the individual setting.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.explanation: Direction perpendicular to the plane, [nx, ny, nz]. It orients the plane and defines its positive side: points toward which the normal points have positive implicit-function values Normal·(x − Origin), points on the other side negative; clip and extract operations use this sign to decide which side to keep. VTK does not normalize the vector, so its length scales the function value.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.label: Normal
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/HyperT.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from [1, 0, 0], a plane perpendicular to the x axis.
pitfalls: A zero vector defines no plane; give at least one non-zero component.

Use a unit-length normal. A longer vector scales the implicit-function values (and the shift produced by Offset), which changes the meaning of value-based settings on the operation, such as slice offsets or a clip value, where the operation has them.

A runtime value replaces a literal setting with an expression that Schemaxis evaluates on each selected visit (one combination of simulation time and active axis values) before this setting is applied; $observe and $sample read upstream nodes after they have been updated on that visit. Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).
$observe and $sample make the named node a dependency, so it must be upstream; pointing back at this node or a consumer creates a cycle (PIPELINE_CYCLE).
A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.
In scene styles and cameras, $axis may only name an axis the scene's nodes already vary; use an explicit camera list for camera-only variation.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/PointM.label: Point Merge Method

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/PointM.explanation: This property specifies which incremental point locator to use for handling duplicate/coincident points.

Uniform Binning (vtkMergePoints): merges output points whose coordinates are exactly identical, using a uniform grid of buckets, so vertices shared by neighbouring output cells appear once and the generated surface or line set is connected. It is ParaView’s initial choice and suits most data. Choose Octree Binning for very unevenly distributed points (strongly refined or adaptive meshes) and Not Merging Points only when speed matters more than connectivity.

Uniform Binning (vtkMergePoints): merges output points whose coordinates are exactly identical, using a uniform grid of buckets, so vertices shared by neighbouring output cells appear once and the generated surface or line set is connected. It is ParaView’s initial choice and suits most data. Choose Octree Binning for very unevenly distributed points (strongly refined or adaptive meshes) and Not Merging Points only when speed matters more than connectivity.
Sizing of the bucket grid used to detect duplicate points. These settings change run time and memory, not the output geometry; omitted settings keep ParaView’s initial values.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/PointM.defaultMeaning: Omitted or {}: Schemaxis assigns none of these settings, so each keeps the native proxy’s initial value described on the individual setting.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/PointM.explanation: Sizing of the bucket grid used to detect duplicate points. These settings change run time and memory, not the output geometry; omitted settings keep ParaView’s initial values.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/PointM.defaultMeaning: Omitted or {}: Schemaxis assigns none of these settings, so each keeps the native proxy’s initial value described on the individual setting.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/PointM.explanation: Number of buckets along x, y and z of the uniform search grid used to find coincident points. It affects speed and memory only, never which points merge (only identical coordinates merge). VTK’s automatic sizing is on by default for this locator and ParaView does not expose it, so whenever the operation supplies an estimated point count the grid is sized from Number of points per bucket instead and Divisions is not used.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/PointM.label: Divisions
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/PointM.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from [50, 50, 50].
pitfalls: Changing Divisions does not merge near-duplicate points; use a cleaning operation with an explicit tolerance for that.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/PointM.explanation: Octree Binning (vtkIncrementalOctreePointLocator): merges exactly coincident points like Uniform Binning, but organizes them in an adaptive octree that subdivides only where points are dense. Choose it when the generated points are very unevenly distributed (for example contours through boundary layers or adaptive meshes), where a uniform grid wastes memory or becomes slow.

Octree Binning (vtkIncrementalOctreePointLocator): merges exactly coincident points like Uniform Binning, but organizes them in an adaptive octree that subdivides only where points are dense. Choose it when the generated points are very unevenly distributed (for example contours through boundary layers or adaptive meshes), where a uniform grid wastes memory or becomes slow.

Octree leaf size and merge tolerance. Leaf size only changes speed; keep Tolerance at 0 so that only exact duplicates merge. Omitted settings keep ParaView’s initial values (128 points per leaf, tolerance 0).

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/PointM.explanation: Not Merging Points (vtkNonMergingPointLocator): inserts every generated point directly without checking for duplicates. It is the fastest option, but each output cell gets its own copy of shared vertices, so the result is not connected (more points, faceted normals, connectivity-based operations see separate pieces). Choose it only when you do not need shared points or will clean the output later.
pitfalls: Downstream smoothing, normals or connectivity filters treat the duplicated vertices as separate; switch to Uniform Binning if the surface looks cracked or shades as facets.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceO.explanation: The values in this property specify a list of current offset values. This can be used to create multiple slices with different centers. Each entry represents a new slice with its center shifted by the offset value. The 'Values Range' information is the range based on the global bounding box, not necessarily on the current slice geometry configuration.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceO.label: Slice Offset Values

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceO.explanation: The values in this property specify a list of current offset values. This can be used to create multiple slices with different centers. Each entry represents a new slice with its center shifted by the offset value. The 'Values Range' information is the range based on the global bounding box, not necessarily on the current slice geometry configuration.

One offset value; each entry yields one cut surface where the slice function equals this value. For a Plane it shifts the cut along the normal by offset times the normal's length (a signed distance in dataset units when the normal has unit length); 0 is the plane itself. Duplicates give coincident slices.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceO.units: Slice-function value (dataset length units for a unit-normal plane)
pitfalls: For a Sphere the function is |x - c|^2 - R^2, so an offset v gives radius sqrt(R^2 + v), not R + v; Cylinder behaves the same way.
Set the list explicitly to get more than one slice or to state the intent; omitted, the plane cut is still made once (offset 0).
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceO.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; the XML declares no default values. In a bounded native probe an omitted list read back [] on a batch run (every node is created before any data exist) and [0] when the upstream already had data, and both produced one cut surface (26 and 28 cells; the plane origin also differed between the two runs, see the SliceType Origin), so an omitted list still cuts once at offset 0.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: This property sets the parameters of the slice function.

A rectangular box region (ParaView’s vtkPVBox): a unit cube scaled by Length, rotated by Rotation about its minimum corner and moved to Position, or, with UseReferenceBounds, the Bounds box transformed in the same way. The implicit function is negative inside and positive outside. Choose it to keep, remove or extract a box-shaped region; slicing or cutting with a box produces the box faces where they cross the data.
pitfalls: ParaView’s initial box may be a unit cube at the origin if the input bounds were not applied; set Position and Length explicitly.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: A rectangular box region (ParaView’s vtkPVBox): a unit cube scaled by Length, rotated by Rotation about its minimum corner and moved to Position, or, with UseReferenceBounds, the Bounds box transformed in the same way. The implicit function is negative inside and positive outside. Choose it to keep, remove or extract a box-shaped region; slicing or cutting with a box produces the box faces where they cross the data.
pitfalls: ParaView’s initial box may be a unit cube at the origin if the input bounds were not applied; set Position and Length explicitly.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: Placement and size of the box. Omitted settings keep ParaView’s initial values, which may cover the whole input.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.defaultMeaning: Omitted or {}: Schemaxis assigns none of these settings, so each keeps the native proxy’s initial value described on the individual setting.

Main forms: {"$axis": name} reads the current sweep value, {"$time": true} the current simulation time, {"$observe": node, "path": [...]} metadata such as bounds or field ranges of an updated upstream node, {"$sample": node, ...} one numeric data value, {"$calc": ...} arithmetic, vector and bounds operations, and {"$call": name, "args": {...}} a registered function such as boundsCentre. The result must still be valid for this setting; see docs/dollar-reference.md.
pitfalls: Constructor settings, such as reader file names, must be constant; a runtime value there fails (DYNAMIC_CONSTRUCTOR).
$observe and $sample make the named node a dependency, so it must be upstream; pointing back at this node or a consumer creates a cycle (PIPELINE_CYCLE).
A marker replaces the whole value; it is not interpolated inside a string.
In scene styles and cameras, $axis may only name an axis the scene's nodes already vary; use an explicit camera list for camera-only variation.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.label: Runtime value

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: Rotation angles [rx, ry, rz] about the x, y and z axes, applied about the box’s local origin (its minimum corner at Position, not its centre; with UseReferenceBounds true, about the coordinate origin). The angles are combined in VTK’s Z-X-Y convention: the box transform is Translate · RotateZ · RotateX · RotateY · Scale.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.label: Rotation
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from [0, 0, 0], an axis-aligned box.
pitfalls: Rotating swings the box around its minimum corner; move Position as well if the box should turn about its centre.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: Chooses how the box is defined. False: the box is a unit cube scaled by Length, rotated about its corner and placed at Position. True: the box starts from Bounds, and Length, Rotation and Position act as scale, rotation and translation relative to it (about the coordinate origin).
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.label: Use reference bounds
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from false.
pitfalls: With true, non-identity Length or Rotation also move a box that lies away from the origin, because they act about the origin, not the box centre.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: An infinite circular cylinder (ParaView’s vtkPVCylinder) of Radius around the line through Center with direction Axis; the implicit function is negative inside and positive outside. It has no end caps, so choose it for pipes, jets, wells or rotating regions whose length need not be bounded; add a second clip if you need a finite length.
pitfalls: The cylinder extends without limit along Axis, so it also affects distant parts of the data on that line.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: Axis line (Center and Axis) and Radius of the cylinder. Omitted settings keep ParaView’s initial values: axis along y and, possibly, a centre and radius derived from the input bounds.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.defaultMeaning: Omitted or {}: Schemaxis assigns none of these settings, so each keeps the native proxy’s initial value described on the individual setting.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: Direction [ax, ay, az] of the cylinder's axis line through Center; the cylinder is infinitely long in both directions. For ordinary datasets ParaView normalizes the vector, so only its direction matters.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.label: Axis
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from [0, 1, 0], the y axis.
pitfalls: A zero vector has no direction; give at least one non-zero component.

The hyper-tree-grid clip (pvClip HyperTreeGridClipper) builds its quadric from the axis components as given, without normalizing, so a non-unit axis distorts the cylinder there; give a unit vector such as [0, 0, 1].
sources: https://gitlab.kitware.com/paraview/paraview/-/raw/v5.13.3/VTKExtensions/FiltersGeneral/vtkPVClipDataSet.cxx (hyper tree grid branch: GetOrientedAxis used unnormalized in SetQuadricCoefficients)

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: An infinite flat plane through Origin, oriented by Normal (ParaView’s vtkPVPlane). It is the usual choice, and ParaView’s initial one for most operations that offer it: use it for planar cuts, clips or selections at any orientation. Where offered, prefer Axis Aligned Plane when the plane must stay exactly perpendicular to x, y or z, and Box, Sphere or Cylinder when the region of interest is closed or curved.
pitfalls: The plane is unbounded: it cuts through every part of the dataset it crosses, including distant parts.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: Direction perpendicular to the plane, [nx, ny, nz]. It orients the plane and defines its positive side: points toward which the normal points have positive implicit-function values Normal·(x − Origin), points on the other side negative; clip and extract operations use this sign to decide which side to keep. VTK does not normalize the vector, so its length scales the function value.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.label: Normal
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from [1, 0, 0], a plane perpendicular to the x axis.
pitfalls: A zero vector defines no plane; give at least one non-zero component.

Use a unit-length normal. A longer vector scales the implicit-function values (and the shift produced by Offset), which changes the meaning of value-based settings on the operation, such as slice offsets or a clip value, where the operation has them.

/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.explanation: A point the plane passes through, as [x, y, z] in the input’s own coordinates. With Normal it defines the infinite plane Normal·(x − Origin) = 0 used to clip, slice, cut or select. Moving Origin along the normal shifts the plane; moving it within the plane changes nothing.
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.label: Origin
/$defs/options-pvSlice/properties/SliceT.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; the XML default is [0, 0, 0], but the plane's bounds domain sets the middle of the input's bounds once data exist (misc_utilities.xml:143-158). A node created after its upstream has data therefore gets the data centre, whereas on a Schemaxis batch run (every node is created before any data exist) the bounds are unset and, by the source, the origin stays [0, 0, 0]. Set it explicitly when the result depends on it.
pitfalls: Coordinates are absolute, not fractions of the model: on a part spanning 0–2000 mm, [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] lies at a corner. Use the model’s own units.
Offset is added on top of Origin along Normal; keep Offset at 0 if Origin should be the exact plane position.

A plane that ParaView keeps perpendicular to a coordinate axis (vtkPVPlane with axis snapping on): any Normal is replaced by the x, y or z axis of its largest component. Choose it for hyper tree grid or AMR slicing, or whenever the cut must be exactly normal to an axis; choose Plane, where offered, for an oblique cut.

/$defs/options-pvSliceWithPlane/properti.explanation: When true, ParaView replaces Normal by the coordinate axis of its largest absolute component, so the plane is always perpendicular to x, y or z. The snapped normal is always positive ([-1, 0, 0] becomes [1, 0, 0]), and tied components are all set to 1 ([1, 1, 0] stays [1, 1, 0]) rather than resolved to one axis. When false, Normal is used as given.
/$defs/options-pvSliceWithPlane/properti.label: Always snap to nearest axis
/$defs/options-pvSliceWithPlane/properti.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from true.
pitfalls: The snap is applied when Normal is set and is not undone when snapping is later turned off (SetAxisAligned re-applies the stored, already snapped normal). For an oblique plane, use the Plane choice where the operation offers it.
ParaView keeps the requested Normal in the property while the plane uses the snapped vector, so Schemaxis readback does not reveal the snap; write a pure axis normal such as [0, 0, 1].

/$defs/options-pvSliceWithPlane/properti.explanation: Direction perpendicular to the plane, [nx, ny, nz]. It orients the plane and defines its positive side: points toward which the normal points have positive implicit-function values Normal·(x − Origin), points on the other side negative; clip and extract operations use this sign to decide which side to keep. VTK does not normalize the vector, so its length scales the function value.

pitfalls: A zero vector defines no plane; give at least one non-zero component.

Use a unit-length normal. A longer vector scales the implicit-function values (and the shift produced by Offset), which changes the meaning of value-based settings on the operation, such as slice offsets or a clip value, where the operation has them.

/$defs/options-pvSliceWithPlane/properti.explanation: An infinite flat plane through Origin, oriented by Normal (ParaView’s vtkPVPlane). It is the usual choice, and ParaView’s initial one for most operations that offer it: use it for planar cuts, clips or selections at any orientation. Where offered, prefer Axis Aligned Plane when the plane must stay exactly perpendicular to x, y or z, and Box, Sphere or Cylinder when the region of interest is closed or curved.
pitfalls: The plane is unbounded: it cuts through every part of the dataset it crosses, including distant parts.

/$defs/options-pvSliceWithPlane/properti.explanation: Position and orientation of the plane: Origin (a point on it), Normal (its orientation and positive side) and Offset (an extra shift along the normal). Origin and Normal decide the result; omitted settings keep ParaView’s initial values, and Origin may be derived from the input bounds, so set both explicitly for reproducible results.
/$defs/options-pvSliceWithPlane/properti.defaultMeaning: Omitted or {}: Schemaxis assigns none of these settings, so each keeps the native proxy’s initial value described on the individual setting.

/$defs/options-pvSliceWithPlane/properti.explanation: Direction perpendicular to the plane, [nx, ny, nz]. It orients the plane and defines its positive side: points toward which the normal points have positive implicit-function values Normal·(x − Origin), points on the other side negative; clip and extract operations use this sign to decide which side to keep. VTK does not normalize the vector, so its length scales the function value.
/$defs/options-pvSliceWithPlane/properti.label: Normal
/$defs/options-pvSliceWithPlane/properti.defaultMeaning: Not set by Schemaxis; ParaView 5.13.3 starts from [1, 0, 0], a plane perpendicular to the x axis.
pitfalls: A zero vector defines no plane; give at least one non-zero component.

Use a unit-length normal. A longer vector scales the implicit-function values (and the shift produced by Offset), which changes the meaning of value-based settings on the operation, such as slice offsets or a clip value, where the operation has them.
